verification.title: b-min-sep Monte Carlo epsilon depends on Rayon thread count with a fixed seed
verification.reasoning: Reproduced end to end. mc.rs:360-378 partitions MC work by rayon::current_num_threads().max(1) and seeds shards seed+tid (remove) / seed+1000+tid (add), so the sample set depends on the machine's core count; bandmf_b_min_sep_prepare_transcripts (mc.rs:174-218) deliberately mirrors the same thread partition, and the Python transcript cache key does not include the thread count. Measured through the native entry with seed=173, coef=[sqrt(0.7),sqrt(0.3)], n=50, p=0.05, sigma=1.0, mc_resolution=5e-3, mc_failure_probability=1e-2: epsilon_at(1e-2) = 1.5788540210820663 (RAYON_NUM_THREADS=1), 1.5938243242558099 (2), 1.8443435849560390 (8) — a 17% swing from core count alone. The sibling balls-in-bins path solves exactly this with fixed 1024-sample shards and shard_seed(seed, shard, add_direction) (balls_in_bins/monte_carlo.rs:43-55) plus a Rust test and packages/opaque-accounting/tests/test_balls_in_bins_reproducible.py; random allocation has an equivalent test. No analogous mechanism or test exists for b_min_sep, which is the default sampler for mf_band. The seed+1000+tid collision only bites above 1000 Rayon workers — real but negligible. Each individual value is still a valid confidence bound for its own sample set, so this is nondeterminism of the reported guarantee, not an invalid one. Not a duplicate: open #666 asks for MC regression vectors (a test gap this defect blocks), #697 (closed) covered prefix tightness and MC-error certification, and the closed #331 fix covered only balls-in-bins.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A team pins a seed for a BandMF + b-min-sep run and gets a different reported epsilon on different hardware: with everything else identical, epsilon_at(1e-2) is 1.579 on 1 Rayon worker, 1.594 on 2, and 1.844 on 8 (measured on this tree). Calibration on a many-core box therefore selects a different noise multiplier than the same configuration on a CI runner, and a published (epsilon, delta, seed) triple cannot be reproduced by a third party. Each value remains a valid confidence bound for the samples it drew, so the failure is silent nondeterminism of the guarantee rather than an invalid bound.

survivors.title: loss_scores/gradient_scores silently score a wrong dataset when canary indices happen to be in range
survivors.claim: The verified scoring path (`_IndexedCanaries.__getitem__` → `self._dataset[int(self._canary_indices[position])]`, _helpers.py:79-81) accepts any `dataset` object with no check that it is the dataset the partition was created from — CoinFlip records neither the dataset size nor any fingerprint. The crafted-canary workflow introduced by PR #751 doubles the number of dataset objects in flight (base `dataset` vs concatenated `audited`, plus `train_data` subsets), and passing the wrong one is only caught when some canary index exceeds its length; otherwise every score is silently computed for the wrong record and one_run accepts the result.
survivors.failure_scenario: cf = coin_flip(audited, num_canaries=4, key=key(3), candidate_indices=range(0,4)) (pool at the head, e.g. crafted canaries prepended); user scores with dataset=cf.train_subset(audited) instead of audited. Because the out-canary removal shifts Subset positions, canary 2 is scored as record 3 and canary 3 as record 4 — demonstrated: wrong scores [-0.0,-1.0,-9.0,-16.0] vs correct [-0.0,-1.0,-4.0,-9.0], and one_run(...) returned OneRunEstimate(n_in=3, n_out=1, auc=0.667) without any error. The resulting epsilon is silently wrong in either direction. With a tail pool (the documented pattern) the same mistake fails loudly with IndexError, which hides the hazard during doc-following development and surfaces it only when the pool placement changes.
evidence: packages/opaque-auditing/src/opaque/api/auditing/attacks/_helpers.py:79-81: `def __getitem__(self, position): return position, self._dataset[int(self._canary_indices[position])]` — no relationship to the partition's dataset is verified; _scoring_loader (:137-156) validates batch_size and reference_scores types only.

packages/opaque-auditing/src/opaque/api/auditing/_coin_flip.py:136-157: CoinFlip stores only num_canaries, canary_indices, _in_mask, in_indices, out_indices — no dataset_size or fingerprint to check against.

Empirical (this session, 4b13d82): head-pool cf over a 20-record dataset scored against its own 19-record train_subset produced shifted, wrong scores that one_run accepted (output quoted in failure_scenario); the same mistake with a tail pool raised IndexError — fail-loud only by accident of index ranges.
The July audit's clean-note (master list, defended-item 12) covered only train_indices set-subtraction, not the scoring path; no OPEN issue tracks this.
survivors.fix_sketch: Record dataset_size (and optionally a cheap content fingerprint of a few canary rows) on CoinFlip at creation; have _scoring_loader assert len(dataset) == cf.dataset_size before building the loader, with an error message naming the concatenated-audited-dataset requirement. This turns both the base-dataset and train-subset mistakes into deterministic failures instead of range-dependent silent corruption.

verification.title: loss_scores/gradient_scores silently score a wrong dataset when canary indices happen to be in range
verification.reasoning: Reproduced verbatim on this tree. With a 20-record dataset, cf = coin_flip(ds, num_canaries=4, key=key(3), candidate_indices=range(0,4)) gives canary_indices [0 1 2 3], out=[2]; scoring against cf.train_subset(ds) (len 19) returned [-0., -1., -9., -16.] instead of the correct [-0., -1., -4., -9.], and one_run accepted it: OneRunEstimate(n_in=3, n_out=1, auc=0.6667) with no error. The chain holds: _helpers.py:79-81 indexes whatever object it is handed, _scoring_loader (:137-156) validates only batch_size and reference_scores types, and CoinFlip (_coin_flip.py:136-157) stores no dataset size or fingerprint, so a one-line len(dataset) == dataset_size guard is unavailable. Severity stays low and I moved affects_epsilon to false: this is a caller mistake against an explicitly documented contract - loss_scores' docstring says 'dataset: The full dataset the partition was created from' and docs/user-guide/auditing.md:276-277 says 'Use the same audited dataset for coin_flip, subset construction, and scoring' - and it corrupts only an empirical audit estimate under that mistake, never a mechanism's guarantee. The finding's real content is the missing cheap defensive check, and the observation that head-placed pools (the crafted-canary layout PR #751 enables) turn a loud IndexError into silent corruption is accurate.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A caller passes the wrong dataset object to loss_scores/gradient_scores - most plausibly cf.train_subset(audited) instead of audited, which the crafted-canary workflow makes easy by putting two dataset objects in flight. _IndexedCanaries indexes the supplied object with the partition's canary indices, so when the pool sits near the head of the dataset the removed out-canaries shift Subset positions and every canary is scored against a different record. Reproduced: wrong scores [-0.,-1.,-9.,-16.] vs correct [-0.,-1.,-4.,-9.], accepted by one_run as OneRunEstimate(n_in=3, n_out=1, auc=0.6667) with no warning. With a tail pool the same mistake raises IndexError, so the hazard is invisible while following the documented layout. Impact is a wrong empirical audit number under a documented-contract violation, not a change to any mechanism's privacy guarantee; fix is to record dataset size (or a fingerprint) on CoinFlip and check it in _scoring_loader.

survivors.title: Lambda-CGD noise stream is unrooted: fold_in(key, step) collides with the caller's documented key space (missed by fix #728)
survivors.claim: Commit 6f6d132a (fix(random)!: namespace mechanism RNG stream roots, #728) established the repo-wide invariant that every mechanism folds a unique string tag into the key it is given before deriving per-step keys ('every stream root Opaque derives for itself is a namespaced string' — noise_allocation.py:25-38; docs/reference/rng.md tag table), and applied it to DP-SGD Gaussian (GAUSSIAN_STREAM_FOLD, _gaussian.py:71), MF dense+streaming (MF_GAUSSIAN_STREAM_FOLD, _engine.py:37,167,395), second-moment, adaptive clipping, and auditing. Lambda-CGD's PRNG-replay noise was missed: _lambda_cgd.py:280 'current_key = rng_fold_in(st._rng_key, step)' and :292 'prev_key = rng_fold_in(st._rng_key, step - 1)' derive privacy-noise generators directly on the caller's integer fold path. Since split(key, n) is defined as fold_in(key, i) (random/_engine.py:127) and the docs explicitly assign integer folds to the caller ('Integers are the caller's... every key split hands back'; rng.md recommends 'noise_key = fold_in(base, step)' and the split loop pattern), any caller that reuses the base key it gave lambda-CGD for an ordinary integer derivation obtains byte-identical torch.Generator streams to the mechanism's privacy noise. The public path is unguarded end to end: mf_gaussian_noise(strategy=lambda_cgd_strategy(...), key=user_key) -> _make_raw_mf_noise (_mf_gaussian_noise.py:131-139, 231-233, no root fold) -> LambdaCgdStrategy.raw_noise_factory (_lambda_cgd.py:152-169) -> fold_in(user_key, step). BiSR, the only other strategy with raw_noise_factory, routes through the rooted _matrix_factorization_noise (_bisr.py:131), so lambda-CGD is the sole surviving instance of the exact defect pattern #728 fixed. The guard test test_stream_root_namespacing.py cannot catch it because it only checks enumerated string constants, and lambda-CGD has none.
survivors.failure_scenario: User writes the documented pattern: base = key(42); passes base to mf_gaussian_noise(strategy=lambda_cgd_strategy(...), key=base) and elsewhere derives step_k via split(base) or fold_in(base, step) for their own generator_from_key draws (dropout, data augmentation, a second mechanism, a logged/released random quantity). Reproduced live: with k = key(42), torch.randn(5, generator=generator_from_key(split(k, 2)[0])) is torch.equal to the lambda-CGD step-0 privacy noise (both [0.9301, 0.2699, 0.5048, -1.2086, -0.0477]). If the colliding stream is observable (released values, deterministic replay of user-side randomness), the DP noise is exactly predictable and the effective epsilon is unbounded, with no warning, error, or accounting signal. Restarting a fresh lambda-CGD mechanism with the same key also byte-replays the previous run's noise (correlated releases the fixed-horizon MF accounting does not model).
evidence: packages/opaque-dpftrl/src/opaque/api/dpftrl/noise/_lambda_cgd.py:280 'current_key = rng_fold_in(st._rng_key, step)' and :292 'prev_key = rng_fold_in(st._rng_key, step - 1)' — no string root; contrast _engine.py:395-397 streaming path 'step_key = rng_fold_in(st._rng_key, MF_GAUSSIAN_STREAM_FOLD, "mf_gaussian_column", step)'.
git show 6f6d132a --stat: #728 touched _engine.py, _second_moment.py, _adaptive.py, _distributed.py, _gaussian.py, _coin_flip.py, noise_allocation.py — _lambda_cgd.py absent.

packages/opaque-engine/src/opaque/api/engine/random/_engine.py:118-127: split(key, n) == fold_in(key, i) for i in range(n); fold_in docstring :71-83 'Integers are the caller's ... Skipping the string root is the failure this convention exists to prevent'.
packages/opaque-engine/src/opaque/api/engine/noise_allocation.py:27-38: 'Integers belong to the caller ...; every stream root Opaque derives for itself is a namespaced string.'
docs/reference/rng.md:206-228: tag table omits lambda-CGD (it has no tag) and recommends caller patterns 'noise_key = fold_in(base, step)', 'fold_in(base, step, rank)'.

Live repro (uv run python on this tree): _make_lambda_cgd_noise(key=key(42)) step-0 output on zero grads is torch.equal to torch.randn(5, generator=generator_from_key(split(key(42), 2)[0])) — BYTE-IDENTICAL: True.

packages/opaque-dpftrl/src/opaque/api/dpftrl/noise/_mf_gaussian_noise.py:114-139 and :231-233 pass the user key verbatim to raw_noise_factory; packages/opaque-engine/tests/rng/test_stream_root_namespacing.py:26-63 enumerates only constant tags, so lambda-CGD is invisible to the guard test.
survivors.fix_sketch: Root the stream: LAMBDA_CGD_STREAM_FOLD = "opaque.dpftrl.lambda_cgd" in _lambda_cgd.py; derive current_key = rng_fold_in(st._rng_key, LAMBDA_CGD_STREAM_FOLD, step) and prev_key = rng_fold_in(st._rng_key, LAMBDA_CGD_STREAM_FOLD, step - 1). This is a breaking noise-stream change (same class as #728, which was already shipped as '!'). Add the tag to docs/reference/rng.md and to _dpftrl_roots() in test_stream_root_namespacing.py; add a domain-separation test that two mechanisms (lambda-CGD + anything) sharing a base key draw non-identical noise, mirroring test_domain_separation.py in opaque-dpsgd.

verification.title: Lambda-CGD noise stream is unrooted: fold_in(key, step) collides with the caller's documented key space (missed by fix #728)
verification.reasoning: Reproduced end to end through the public API. _lambda_cgd.py:280 does current_key = rng_fold_in(st._rng_key, step) and :292 prev_key = rng_fold_in(st._rng_key, step - 1) with no string root, while every sibling mechanism roots itself (_engine.py:396 with MF_GAUSSIAN_STREAM_FOLD; _gaussian.py:407; _adaptive.py:113; _second_moment.py:92,101). The public path is unguarded: mf_gaussian_noise validates only the key type and passes it verbatim (_mf_gaussian_noise.py:131-139) to _make_raw_mf_noise (:231-237), which hands it straight to LambdaCgdStrategy.raw_noise_factory (:152-169). BiSR is the only other raw_noise_factory and it routes through the rooted _matrix_factorization_noise (_bisr.py:131-137), so lambda-CGD is the sole surviving instance. split(key, n) is exactly (fold_in(key, i)) (random/_engine.py:118-127), so the mechanism's step keys ARE keys a caller gets from an ordinary derivation. Live repro: mf_gaussian_noise(zeros template, lambda_cgd_strategy(lambda_=0.5, normalized=False), n_steps=4, noise_multiplier=1.0, key=key(42)) step-0 noise is tensor([0.9301, 0.2699, 0.5048, -1.2086, -0.0477]) and torch.randn(5, generator=generator_from_key(split(key(42),2)[0])) is byte-identical (torch.equal True). The guard test cannot see it: test_stream_root_namespacing.py:26-63 enumerates only declared string constants and lambda-CGD declares none. docs/reference/rng.md:214-222 additionally asserts 'opaque.dpftrl.mf_gaussian' is occupied by mf_gaussian_noise, which is false for this strategy, so a careful reader is told the stream is rooted when it is not. Two corrections to the report: no in-repo default collides (the trainer's DP-FTRL branch passes key(a.seed) at _dp_trainer.py:1576, adaptive-clipping quantile noise is string-rooted, and MF rejects adaptive clipping anyway), so exploitation needs caller-side key reuse; and 'restarting with the same key replays the noise' is true of every deterministically seeded mechanism, not specific to lambda-CGD, so I dropped it. Kept high: an unrooted privacy-noise stream on a public path violates a documented, test-guarded invariant the repo shipped a breaking fix (#728) to establish, and nothing - test, error, or accountant - reports the collision.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A caller uses lambda-CGD through the public factory - mf_gaussian_noise(params, lambda_cgd_strategy(...), n_steps=T, noise_multiplier=nm, key=base) - and, following docs/reference/rng.md:224-227, derives their own torch generators from the same base with integer folds (split(base) or fold_in(base, step)) for dropout, augmentation, a second mechanism, or any logged/released random quantity. Because _lambda_cgd.py:280 derives the DP noise generator as fold_in(base, step) with no mechanism root, those streams are byte-identical to the privacy noise: verified live, step-0 noise == torch.randn(5, generator=generator_from_key(split(key(42),2)[0])). If the colliding caller-side stream is observable, the injected DP noise for that step is exactly recoverable and the guarantee for the affected releases is void, with no warning, error, or accounting signal. No shipped Opaque path collides today (the trainer's other torch streams are string-rooted), so this is a latent public-API defect rather than a live epsilon loss; the fix is one line - root the stream with a namespaced tag, add it to the rng.md table and to test_stream_root_namespacing.py - and is breaking for reproducibility of existing lambda-CGD runs.

survivors.title: Samplers seed numpy RNG from the raw key with no domain separation (same defect class as #728, sibling surface)
survivors.claim: The samplers consume the caller's key without any mechanism root: PoissonSampler does 'self.generator = np.random.default_rng(key.seed)' (_poisson.py:108), balls-in-bins does 'generator = np.random.default_rng(key.seed)' (_balls_in_bins.py:103), and random allocation does 'rng = np.random.default_rng(fold_in(self._key, epoch).seed)' (_random_allocation.py:125) — a bare integer fold on the caller's path. Under the convention #728 shipped ('a mechanism that draws randomness folds one unique string tag into the key it was given', rng.md:208-210), sampling is a randomness-drawing mechanism whose stream should be namespaced: two different samplers built from the same key draw identical PCG64 streams, and random-allocation's epoch stream is byte-identical to any caller-side np.random.default_rng(fold_in(key, epoch).seed). Sampling randomness is amplification-relevant, so stream reuse is not merely a reproducibility nit. Mitigating factors keep this low: the trainer derives the sampler key from data_seed/seed with its own string fold on the restart path (_dp_trainer.py:3688-3703), only one sampler is built per run, and the torch-side noise streams are blake2b-separated from key.seed, so no in-repo default collides.
survivors.failure_scenario: A manual-loop user holds one master key and passes it to both a Poisson sampler and a balls-in-bins sampler (e.g. comparing samplers, or train + canary-insertion sampling): both consume np.random.default_rng(key.seed) and draw the identical stream, so the two 'independent' sampling processes are perfectly correlated — participation patterns coincide and any analysis multiplying their probabilities (or treating one as fresh randomness) is wrong. Similarly, a caller that publishes anything derived from default_rng(fold_in(key, epoch).seed) has published the random-allocation assignment stream, voiding the allocation's secrecy assumption. Silent in all cases.
evidence: packages/opaque-dpsgd/src/opaque/api/dpsgd/sampling/_poisson.py:108 'self.generator = np.random.default_rng(key.seed)'.
packages/opaque-dpftrl/src/opaque/api/dpftrl/sampling/_balls_in_bins.py:103-105 'generator = np.random.default_rng(key.seed); assignments = generator.integers(0, num_bins, size=self._num_samples)'.
packages/opaque-dpsgd/src/opaque/api/dpsgd/sampling/_random_allocation.py:125 'rng = np.random.default_rng(fold_in(self._key, epoch).seed)' — integer-only fold on the caller's path.
docs/reference/rng.md:208-210 states every mechanism roots itself with a unique string tag; the tag table (rng.md:214-222) lists no sampler tags.

Trainer wiring is safe by construction, not by the samplers: _dp_trainer.py:3688 'sampler_key = key(a.data_seed if a.data_seed is not None else a.seed)' with a string fold only on the ignore_data_skip restart path (:3693-3697).
survivors.fix_sketch: Give each sampler a namespaced root before seeding numpy: e.g. default_rng(fold_in(key, "opaque.dpsgd.poisson").seed), default_rng(fold_in(key, "opaque.dpftrl.balls_in_bins").seed), and fold_in(self._key, "opaque.dpsgd.random_allocation", epoch) — preserving state-dict compatibility via the stored original key. Register the tags in rng.md and the namespacing test. Note this changes sampling streams (breaking, like #728).

verification.title: Samplers seed numpy RNG from the raw key with no domain separation (same defect class as #728, sibling surface)
verification.reasoning: The code facts are exactly as stated and the surface is slightly larger than reported: np.random.default_rng is seeded from a bare key.seed at dpsgd/_poisson.py:108, dpftrl/_poisson.py:111, dpftrl/_b_min_sep.py:73, dpftrl/_balls_in_bins.py:103 and dpsgd/_k_out_of_t.py:58, and from an integer-only fold at dpsgd/_random_allocation.py:125. Under the convention fold_in's own docstring states (random/_engine.py:71-83, 'A mechanism that draws randomness folds one unique string tag into the key it was given') and docs/reference/rng.md:208-222 (whose tag table lists no sampler), samplers are randomness-drawing mechanisms and are unrooted. The mitigations the reporter lists all check out: the trainer builds one sampler per run from key(a.data_seed or a.seed) with a string fold only on the ignore_data_skip restart path (_dp_trainer.py:3686-3703), and the torch-side noise streams go through generator_from_key (seed % MAX_TORCH_SEED into a torch Generator), a different PRNG family from numpy's PCG64, so no in-repo default draws a colliding stream. I moved affects_epsilon to false: unlike finding 68 there is no path where an honest caller's stream aliases a sampler's, the amplification analysis does not require the sampling stream to be unpredictable to the key holder, and the reporter's scenarios are either contrived (publishing default_rng(fold_in(key, epoch).seed) output) or benign (two samplers seeded identically is what a caller comparing samplers would want). Real content: a convention/hygiene deviation the namespacing guard test structurally cannot see, worth fixing alongside 68 while the tag table is being edited.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: All samplers seed numpy from the caller's key with no mechanism root, so two samplers constructed from one key draw the identical PCG64 stream (perfectly correlated participation patterns), and RandomAllocationSampler's per-epoch assignment stream is byte-identical to a caller's own np.random.default_rng(fold_in(key, epoch).seed). This is a documented-convention violation (rng.md:208-210 requires a unique string root per randomness-drawing mechanism; the tag table lists no sampler) that the stream-root guard test cannot detect. No in-repo path collides - the trainer builds one sampler per run and the torch noise streams use a different PRNG family - and no realistic honest usage turns this into a wrong or unsound epsilon, so the impact is reproducibility/hygiene, not privacy loss.

survivors.title: _compile_with_fullgraph_fallback catches every Exception on first call, masking non-compile failures as compile fallbacks
survivors.claim: The compiled DP grad transform wrapper's first-call handler is 'except Exception as e' (_dp_trainer.py:213): ANY exception raised during the first execution of the fullgraph=True compiled grad_fn — an MPS/CUDA OOM, a data-dependent runtime error (bad labels, non-finite loss check), a bug in a user loss closure — is logged as 'torch.compile fullgraph=True failed (...); falling back to fullgraph=False' and the entire step is silently re-executed under a fullgraph=False recompile (:220-221). Genuine errors will usually re-raise from the fallback so nothing is permanently swallowed, but the first failure's identity is misattributed to torch.compile, the step body runs twice (doubling peak-memory pressure exactly when the first failure was an OOM), and a first-call-only transient error (e.g. an inductor-numerics-triggered assert that eager does not hit) is permanently absorbed with only a misleading compile warning. grad_fn is functional (state passed and returned), so the double execution itself does not corrupt clipping or noise state.
survivors.failure_scenario: torch_compile=True on MPS; the first training step OOMs inside the compiled vmap(grad)+clip transform. The user sees 'torch.compile fullgraph=True failed (OutOfMemoryError: ...)' — pointing them at compile flags — while the wrapper immediately re-runs the full forward/backward under a fresh fullgraph=False compilation on an already-exhausted allocator. Debugging is misdirected and the retry can push a borderline configuration over the memory cliff.
evidence: packages/opaque-transformers/src/opaque/api/transformers/trainer/_dp_trainer.py:211-221: 'try: return full(*args, **kwargs) / except Exception as e: log.warning("torch.compile fullgraph=True failed (%s: %s); falling back...") / fallback = torch.compile(fn, ..., fullgraph=False) / return fallback(*args, **kwargs)'.

The docstring (:192-201) motivates the catch as a graph-break fallback, but graph-break failures under fullgraph=True surface as torch._dynamo.exc.Unsupported / BackendCompilerFailed — a narrow set, not Exception.
Interaction with OOM handling: the trainer's collective OOM logic (:2050-2084) only sees the exception the wrapper re-raises from the fallback path, after a second full execution.
survivors.fix_sketch: Narrow the catch to compile-classified failures (torch._dynamo.exc.TorchDynamoException / BackendCompilerFailed / Unsupported), and explicitly re-raise torch.OutOfMemoryError without retry so the trainer's OOM path sees it first-hand. Keep the lazy fallback semantics otherwise.

verification.title: _compile_with_fullgraph_fallback catches every Exception on first call, masking non-compile failures as compile fallbacks
verification.reasoning: The code is exactly as cited: _dp_trainer.py:203-223 compiles with fullgraph=True and the wrapper's first-call handler is a bare 'except Exception as e' that logs 'torch.compile fullgraph=True failed (...); falling back to fullgraph=False for subsequent steps.' then immediately re-executes the whole step under a fresh fullgraph=False compile. So any first-call exception - OOM, a data-dependent RuntimeError, a bug in the user's loss closure - is reported as a torch.compile failure and the step body runs twice. Consequences are real but bounded: a genuine error re-raises from the fallback (so nothing is permanently swallowed except a first-call-only transient), and I confirmed the double execution is harmless to privacy state - the compiled callable is the vmap(grad)+clip transform from _create_grad_fn (:4121-4123, :4125-4145), whose clipping/noise state is threaded functionally and whose adaptive-clipping quantile keys are derived from the step counter rather than a live generator, so re-running reproduces the same randomness. The OOM interaction is the substantive harm: the trainer's collective OOM handling only sees the exception re-raised from the fallback, i.e. after a second full execution on an already-exhausted allocator. Note the docstring (:192-201) frames the broad catch as deliberate, and narrowing it is awkward because torch.compile surfaces failures as Unsupported, BackendCompilerFailed, InternalTorchDynamoError and plain RuntimeError. Confirmed as a diagnosability/robustness defect at low severity, not a correctness bug.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: With torch_compile=True, any exception raised the first time the fullgraph=True grad transform executes is caught by the bare 'except Exception' at _dp_trainer.py:213, logged as a torch.compile fullgraph failure, and the entire step is re-run under a freshly compiled fullgraph=False variant. On a first-step OOM (the realistic case on MPS) the user is pointed at compile flags rather than memory, and the retry re-executes the full forward/backward on an already-exhausted allocator before the trainer's OOM handling ever sees the error; a first-call-only transient is absorbed entirely behind a misleading warning. No DP state is corrupted by the double execution - the compiled transform is functional and its RNG derivations are step-indexed, so the retry reproduces identical clipping and noise - so the impact is misdirected debugging plus doubled peak-memory pressure at exactly the wrong moment.

survivors.title: StepPerf.memory_peak_gb on MPS is the run-wide reserved high-water, not the per-step peak its docstring claims
survivors.claim: On MPS, get_memory_stats reports peak_gb = torch.mps.driver_allocated_memory() (the driver's monotonic reserved high-water, _memory.py:162-171) and step_perf deliberately never resets it per step (peak_memory_trackable is False for MPS — _capabilities.py:124-129, gate at _memory.py:414). The internal comments document this accurately, but the user-facing StepPerf dataclass docstring says 'memory_peak_gb: Peak GPU memory during the step' (_memory.py:275) and MemoryStats marks the value exact_peak=True (:174). So per-step logs on MPS (StepPerf.to_dict -> 'memory_peak_gb', wandb examples in the module docstring) show a monotonically non-decreasing run-cumulative figure labeled as a per-step peak, and per-step regressions/comparisons on MPS are meaningless while looking precise. CUDA behavior (true per-step peak, reset each step) diverges silently from MPS behavior under the same field name.

survivors.title: DataLoader prefetch advances the allocation cursor past global_step, so resume misaligns the accountant's allocation epochs with the sampler's
survivors.claim: RandomAllocationSampler._consumed is incremented inside __iter__ when the DataLoader pulls an index list, not when the trainer consumes the batch. With dataloader_num_workers > 0 PyTorch prefetches num_workers * prefetch_factor batches, so _consumed runs ahead of the trainer's global_step. The checkpoint stores that advanced cursor (`sampler_state = opaque_state_dict(ctx.current_sampler)`), and on resume the sampler continues from it while the accountant continues from global_step. From then on accountant step j is served by sampler slot j+p, so the accountant's modelled allocation epochs [m*b,(m+1)*b) straddle two of the sampler's actual epochs and a record can participate twice inside one modelled epoch. The reported epsilon is then below the epsilon of the mechanism that actually ran.
survivors.failure_scenario: num_bins=8, sigma=1.0, dataloader_num_workers=2 (prefetch_factor=2 => p=4). Train 8 steps, checkpoint (global_step=8, sampler.consumed=12), resume, train 8 more. Accountant charges pld_at(16) = alloc(8) (x) alloc(8) => eps=3.127790 at delta=1e-5. What actually ran is sampler slots 0..7 (one full epoch) then slots 12..19 (last 4 slots of epoch 1 plus first 4 slots of epoch 2), i.e. alloc(8) (x) prefix(8,4) (x) prefix(8,4) => eps=3.392558 at delta=1e-5 (5.116893 vs 4.687320 at delta=1e-8). That is an 8.5% under-report; every further resume adds another misaligned boundary (offsets accumulate as p, 2p, 3p...). PoissonSampler is immune (per-step i.i.d. draws) and KOutOfTSampler is only made conservative by the same offset, so this is specific to the per-epoch allocation scheme wired in by PR #307.

Measured with torch DataLoader (scratchpad/prefetch.py): `num_workers=0 after 1 batches: sampler.consumed=1` vs `num_workers=2 after 1 batches: sampler.consumed=5` — a fixed 4-slot lead.

survivors.title: RandomAllocationSampler derives its per-epoch stream with a bare integer fold, colliding with the split()-derived roots the trainer hands the noise and adaptive-clipping mechanisms
survivors.claim: `rng = np.random.default_rng(fold_in(self._key, epoch).seed)` derives the allocation with an integer-only fold and no string domain tag. `opaque.random.fold_in`'s own docstring states that a mechanism "folds one unique string tag into the key it was given, once" and that skipping the string root is "the failure this convention exists to prevent". Because `split(k)` is defined as `fold_in(k, i)`, the trainer's `quantile_noise_key, gradient_noise_key = split(gradient_noise_key)` produces exactly the sampler's epoch-0 and epoch-1 keys. Today nothing breaks, because the Gaussian noise and adaptive-clipping mechanisms apply a further string fold before drawing, so no terminal stream repeats; but the allocation stream sits in the shared integer-fold namespace, so any future mechanism handed the same base key and deriving `fold_in(key, step)` would draw the allocation's bits with nothing to signal it.
survivors.failure_scenario: With `clipping_mode='adaptive'` and default `data_seed=None`, seed=42: the sampler's epoch-0 key seed is 6663219682538052210 and `split(key(42))[0].seed` (the AdaClip quantile-noise root) is the same 6663219682538052210; epoch-1 equals the gradient-noise root 2142789487919306769. Sampling randomness and noise randomness are then deterministic functions of one another's root key rather than being drawn from separated namespaces — the property amplification proofs assume of the sampling coins.

survivors.title: The O(G^2) allocation transform is recomputed from scratch on every distinct step count, making per-log-boundary epsilon_at cost tens of seconds
survivors.claim: `pld_at` is memoised by `horizon_pld_cache(maxsize=16)` keyed on `n_steps`, but the expensive part — `_native.random_allocation_gaussian_pld(noise_multiplier, self.num_bins, 1, native_cfg)` — depends only on `(noise_multiplier, num_bins, config)` and is identical for every `n_steps`. verification.title: The O(G^2) allocation transform is recomputed from scratch on every distinct step count, making per-log-boundary epsilon_at cost tens of seconds
verification.reasoning: Verified. RandomAllocation.pld_at builds the epoch PLD inside the method (_random_allocation.py:145-151) even though _native.random_allocation_gaussian_pld(noise_multiplier, num_bins, 1, native_cfg) depends only on (nm, num_bins, config); horizon_pld_cache keys on (config, _pld_cache_key(n_steps), n_steps) (_pld_cache.py:242) so every distinct n_steps is a miss. PerStep.repeated_pld(count) forwards straight to pld_at(count) (composition/_per_step.py:60-76), and _maybe_log_save_evaluate re-wraps and calls ctx.accounting.epsilon_at(ctx.target_delta) at every should_log boundary (_dp_trainer.py:3958-3960), so the step count - and therefore the cache key - is different at each boundary. I timed the native primitive on this machine (scratchpad/timing.py, default max_conv_grid=32768): num_bins=64 15.1 s, num_bins=256 24.1 s, num_bins=1024 21.2 s per call, same order as reported. The transform is O(G^2) per convolution with G capped at 32768, which explains the cost. NativeCache exists (core/_native_cache.py) but grep shows its only user is the DP-FTRL b-min-sep transcript cache; nothing registers the random-allocation epoch PLD. Severity kept at low: no privacy consequence, the recomputation is in the conservative-neutral direction, and users can raise logging_steps - but it does make random_allocation impractical in the trainer at default logging cadence.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A random_allocation run with num_bins in the hundreds pays a full O(max_conv_grid^2) epoch-PLD build on every epsilon_at at a new step count, because pld_at memoises on n_steps while the expensive term depends only on (noise_multiplier, num_bins, config). Measured here: 15.1 s at num_bins=64, 24.1 s at 256, 21.2 s at 1024 per call with the default max_conv_grid=32768. _maybe_log_save_evaluate queries epsilon at every should_log boundary and _predict_stop_step adds ~log2(horizon) probes at setup, so a 3000-step run with logging_steps=10 spends hours in the accountant recomputing an identical epoch PLD. No epsilon impact - purely wasted compute.

survivors.title: Module docstring claims the discretisation error does not accumulate across the exponentiation-by-squaring convolutions; the measured over-estimate grows with t
survivors.claim: The header states "Crucially the discretisation error does **not** accumulate across them, which is what makes large `t` tractable." What does not accumulate is the *grid size* (`conv` renormalises the anchor and keeps `n` fixed — geom.rs:200-208). The error does accumulate: `conv` rounds every off-grid sum up to the next geometric grid point, so each of the floor(log2 t)+popcount(t)-1 convolutions can inflate the value by a factor up to e^alpha, i.e. the loss by up to alpha per convolution. The crate's own `test_larger_max_conv_grid_tightens_bound` encodes that the bound depends on the grid resolution.
survivors.failure_scenario: A reader sizing `max_conv_grid` for a large-t production run concludes the bound is grid-insensitive and leaves it at the default. Against an independent deterministic reference (value-preserving log-grid convolution, scratchpad/exact_ref.py) the full-epoch over-estimate at sigma=1.0, eps=0.5 grows monotonically with t: ratio 1.0043 at t=8, 1.0084 at t=16, 1.0238 at t=64 — roughly the predicted log2(t)*alpha behaviour, not a constant.
evidence: packages/opaque-accounting/src/amplification/random_allocation.rs:13-15 — "Crucially the discretisation error does **not** accumulate across them".

packages/opaque-accounting/src/pld/pmf/geom.rs:205-209 — `let log_v_min = directed_log_add(a.log_v_min, b.log_v_min, dir);` with `directed_next(...)` applied per convolution, and geom.rs:270-278 rounds each placed sum with `pos.ceil()` under `Rounding::Up`.

packages/opaque-accounting/src/amplification/random_allocation.rs:780-801 — `test_larger_max_conv_grid_tightens_bound` asserts a finer grid gives a strictly tighter epsilon, i.e. the error is grid-dependent.
Measured against an independent reference (scratchpad/exact_ref.py + exact_full.py) at sigma=1.0, eps=0.5: t=8 ratio 1.0043, t=16 ratio 1.0084, t=64 ratio 1.0238.
survivors.fix_sketch: Reword to "the grid size does not grow across them" and state the actual error budget (bounded by roughly (floor(log2 t)+popcount(t)-1) * alpha in absolute loss), so users can size `max_conv_grid` against a stated accuracy target.

verification.title: Module docstring claims the discretisation error does not accumulate across the exponentiation-by-squaring convolutions; the measured over-estimate grows with t
verification.reasoning: The docstring at packages/opaque-accounting/src/amplification/random_allocation.rs:13-15 does say 'Crucially the discretisation error does **not** accumulate across them, which is what makes large t tractable.' What is actually invariant is the grid: GeomPmf::conv keeps n = max(self.n(), other.n()) and re-anchors log_v_min = directed_log_add(a.log_v_min, b.log_v_min, dir) (geom.rs:196-208), so the bin count does not grow. The error does accumulate: convolution_index_table and the place closure both round each off-grid sum with pos.ceil() under Rounding::Up (geom.rs:180-186, 267-280), so each of the floor(log2 t) squarings plus popcount-1 multiplies in self_conv (geom.rs:336-356) can inflate the value by up to one grid ratio. I verified accumulation independently of the reporter's reference implementation, by varying only max_conv_grid: eps at sigma=1.0, delta=1e-5 for one full epoch, coarse grid (1024) minus fine grid (4096), is +0.0159 at t=2, +0.0154 at t=4, +0.0179 at t=8, +0.0233 at t=16, +0.0478 at t=64, +0.0743 at t=256 - i.e. 0.43% relative at t=2 rising to 21% at t=256. The crate's own test_larger_max_conv_grid_tightens_bound (random_allocation.rs:780-801) already encodes the grid dependence. Confirmed as a documentation defect only: the rounding is directional and conservative, so the error inflates epsilon rather than deflating it, hence affects_epsilon=false and severity low. I did not reproduce the reporter's specific ratios (1.0043/1.0084/1.0238) against their external reference, and note their 'roughly log2(t)*alpha' characterisation does not fit their own numbers; the growth is real but its functional form is unverified.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A reader sizing max_conv_grid for a large-t run takes the header at its word, concludes the bound is insensitive to the convolution grid, and leaves the default. In fact each conv rounds every off-grid sum up to the next geometric grid point, so the over-estimate grows with the number of convolutions. Holding everything else fixed and changing only max_conv_grid from 4096 to 1024 inflates the one-epoch epsilon (sigma=1.0, delta=1e-5) by +0.016 at t=2 but +0.074 at t=256 - 0.4% versus 21% relative. The error is conservative (epsilon over-stated), so this is a docs-accuracy and tuning-guidance defect, not a privacy one.

survivors.title: Calibration and the runtime accountant still disagree for Monte-Carlo DP-FTRL accountants: calibrated runs finish above the requested epsilon
survivors.claim: cal.calibrate() runs every probe -- and computes the CalibrateResult.achieved it returns -- inside `with _use_discretization(probe_config)`, where `mc_failure_probability = overall/(max_iterations+2)` (1e-6/102). For Monte-Carlo PLDs that config resolves to ~16% more MC samples (3,417,797 vs 2,940,252) and therefore a *tighter* confidence-bounded epsilon than the module-default config the training loop, `TrainOutput.metrics['privacy_epsilon']` and `accountant.json` are evaluated under. calibrate() never re-checks the chosen parameter under the overall config, so it returns a noise multiplier whose epsilon under the library's own default query config exceeds the user's budget. This is the same calibration-vs-runtime split the July audit found (uncached vs cached process), reappearing as a discretization-context split, and it hits the auto-selected sampler for 5 of 6 MF mechanisms.
survivors.failure_scenario: TrainingArguments(privacy_noise_mechanism='mf_band', privacy_target_epsilon=3.0, privacy_target_delta=1e-5) -> sampling_mode resolves to 'b_min_sep' (_SAMPLER_BY_MECHANISM). DPTrainer.train() calibrates nm=1.0800457763671871, records state.privacy_calibration_achieved_epsilon=2.997967857920426 (<= 3.0, converged=True), trains the full 16-step horizon, and returns metrics['privacy_epsilon']=3.012610878157025 -- above the requested budget. No exception, no warning, and calibrated mode has no stop-at-epsilon at all. Same run for mf_blt/balls_in_bins: achieved 2.9997315463338556, reported 3.0013096663687606. mf_bsr/balls_in_bins: achieved 2.997958944912822, reported 3.0125598920718843.
evidence: calibration.py:296-313: `overall_config = get_discretization(); probe_count = max_iterations + 2; probe_config = replace(overall_config, mc_failure_probability=(overall_config.mc_failure_probability / probe_count)); with _use_discretization(probe_config): result = _calibrate_impl(...)` -- `result.achieved` is produced entirely inside that context.

calibration.py:314-325: after the search only `final_pld` is inspected and `result.mc_failure_probability` is stamped; `result.achieved` is never re-evaluated under `overall_config` and the budget is never re-checked there.

_dp_trainer.py:4374-4389: the trainer passes only budget/objective/bounds/tolerance and stores `result.achieved` into `state.privacy_calibration_achieved_epsilon`; _dp_trainer.py:1931 `final_epsilon = ctx.accounting.epsilon_at(ctx.target_delta)` runs under the default config.

RUN (scratchpad/tc_probe.py, mf_band+b_min_sep, N=16, q=1/16, delta=1e-5, target 3.0): calibrate() achieved = 2.9974753177482585; the SAME process at the SAME param evaluated under probe_config = 2.9974753177482585 (bit-for-bit equal -> proves the context is the cause); evaluated under the default config = 3.01083836210856 (> target).

RUN (scratchpad/tc_e2e2.py, real DPTrainer, tiny LM, 64 examples, batch 4, 16 steps): mf_band+b_min_sep overshoot +0.012611; mf_blt+balls_in_bins +0.001310; mf_bsr+balls_in_bins +0.012560; mf_band+poisson -0.001837 (analytic, exact match); gaussian+poisson -0.000744 (analytic, exact match). For every MC case 'same process, default config' equals the trainer-reported final epsilon exactly.

RUN: DiscretizationConfig(mc_failure_probability=1e-6).resolved_num_mc_samples = 2940252 vs (1e-6/102) -> 3417797, so the probe bound is systematically tighter, i.e. the bias is always in the unsafe direction.

Contract violated in docs/user-guide/accounting.md:429-439: 'For privacy-loss budgets ... the returned metric is at or below the target ... it raises RuntimeError instead of returning an under-noised parameter.'
survivors.fix_sketch: After `_calibrate_impl` returns, re-evaluate `budget.evaluate(process(result.param))` under `overall_config` (outside the probe context) and set `result.achieved` from that value; if it is not privacy-safe, continue bisecting from the safe side under the overall config (or raise) instead of returning. Alternatively run the whole search under `overall_config` and spend the union-bound slack by tightening the *target* rather than the probe's failure probability. Either way the trainer should assert `state.privacy_calibration_achieved_epsilon >= ctx.accounting.epsilon_at(target_delta)` at end of training and fail loudly otherwise.

verification.title: Calibration and the runtime accountant still disagree for Monte-Carlo DP-FTRL accountants: calibrated runs finish above the requested epsilon
verification.reasoning: The mechanical chain reproduces exactly, but the reporter's safety framing is wrong and the severity must come down. Reproduced: I ran scratchpad/tc_probe.py unchanged and got calibrate() param 1.1144531249999998, achieved 2.9974753177482585 (<= target 3.0), the same process re-evaluated under the probe config 2.9974753177482585 (bit-for-bit equal, proving the discretization context is the cause), and under the module-default config 3.01083836210856 - an overshoot of +0.0108 over the requested 3.0. calibration.py:296-313 does run every probe and produce result.achieved inside `with _use_discretization(probe_config)` where mc_failure_probability = overall/(max_iterations+2), and 314-325 only inspects final_pld and stamps result.mc_failure_probability without re-evaluating achieved under overall_config. What refutes the 'unsafe direction' claim: that division is a deliberate union bound, and it is sound. Each probe's Monte-Carlo bound holds with probability 1 - beta/probe_count, so all probes hold simultaneously with probability 1 - beta; the selected parameter's achieved value is therefore a valid (1-beta)-confidence UPPER bound on the true epsilon, and a stronger one than the default config would give. packages/opaque-dpftrl/tests/accounting/test_b_min_sep.py:241-256 (test_calibration_reports_one_overall_mc_confidence_budget) pins exactly that intent, and resolved_num_mc_samples (discretization/config.rs:150-180) picks the smallest n whose unresolved tail is <= mc_resolution, so both configs produce valid bands of the same nominal width - the probe one is just less noisy. Consequently the calibrated noise multiplier is NOT under-noised: with confidence >= 1-1e-6 the run's true epsilon is <= 2.9975 <= 3.0. The reporter's evidence line 'the probe bound is systematically tighter, i.e. the bias is always in the unsafe direction' is a non sequitur - a tighter valid bound is what the confidence budget was spent on. The documented contract in docs/user-guide/accounting.md:429-439 is about the returned metric (result.achieved), which does satisfy 'at or below the target'; I found no documented guarantee that TrainOutput.metrics['privacy_epsilon'] stays under target. What remains, and is worth fixing, is a real reporting inconsistency: the trainer's final_epsilon (_dp_trainer.py:1931, persisted into metrics at 1954 and into accountant.json) is a looser bound computed under a different discretization context than the one the run was calibrated in, so it can print a number above the user's budget with no warning and no reconciliation between the two figures. That is user-visible and confusing but conservative, so severity medium and affects_epsilon corrected to false. Not a duplicate of #329/#666/#697, none of which describes the calibration-probe-versus-runtime discretization split.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: TrainingArguments(privacy_noise_mechanism='mf_band', privacy_target_epsilon=3.0, privacy_target_delta=1e-5) resolves sampling_mode to 'b_min_sep', a Monte-Carlo accountant. calibrate() searches inside `with _use_discretization(probe_config)` (mc_failure_probability 1e-6/102) and returns achieved=2.9974753177482585 <= 3.0, which is stamped into state.privacy_calibration_achieved_epsilon. The trainer then runs and reports metrics['privacy_epsilon'] via ctx.accounting.epsilon_at() under the module-default config, where the same process evaluates to 3.01083836210856 - above the requested budget, with no warning. Both numbers are valid upper confidence bounds on the same true epsilon and the calibration bound is the tighter one, so the run is NOT under-noised and the privacy guarantee (eps <= 3.0 at confidence 1-1e-6) holds; the defect is that the library publishes, persists and cards a looser second number that contradicts the budget it just calibrated to, and never reconciles the two. Reproduced bit-for-bit (achieved 2.9974753177482585, default-config 3.01083836210856, overshoot +0.010838).

survivors.title: Stop-at-epsilon is not enforced per step for the Monte-Carlo DP-FTRL samplers (the auto defaults for 5 of 6 MF mechanisms), so a fixed-noise run blows through privacy_target_epsilon by 6.8x with no signal
survivors.claim: The per-step stop-at-epsilon predictor (`predict_stop_step`, the fix tracked by issue #392 'Enforce stop-at-epsilon on every accounted step', listed CLOSED) is gated on `a.sampling_mode not in ('b_min_sep', 'balls_in_bins')`. Those two are exactly the samplers `_SAMPLER_BY_MECHANISM` auto-selects for mf_band, mf_blt, mf_bisr, mf_bsr and mf_lambda_cgd. For them `ctx.stop_at_step` stays None and the only stop mechanism is the fallback inside `_maybe_log_save_evaluate`, which runs only when `control.should_log` is set -- i.e. every `logging_steps` (default 500) and never at all when `logging_strategy='no'`. So the DP-FTRL default configuration is precisely the configuration where the budget cap is weakest.
survivors.failure_scenario: TrainingArguments(privacy_noise_mechanism='mf_band', privacy_noise_multiplier=1.0, privacy_target_epsilon=0.5, max_steps=16) with stock logging (logging_strategy='steps', logging_steps=500). sampling_mode resolves to 'b_min_sep'. The run executes and accounts all 16 steps, returns metrics['privacy_epsilon']=3.407208272767909 -- 6.8x the requested cap -- and leaves state.privacy_target_epsilon_reached=False. Any MF run shorter than logging_steps never evaluates the stop condition; longer runs evaluate it only every 500 accounted steps, so the overshoot window is up to 499 steps of budget.

_dp_trainer.py:3955-3985: the fallback stop is inside `if ctrl.should_log:` and additionally requires `ctx.stop_at_step is None`.
_training_arguments.py:171-179 `_SAMPLER_BY_MECHANISM`: mf_band->b_min_sep, mf_blt/mf_bisr/mf_bsr/mf_lambda_cgd->balls_in_bins.
_training_arguments.py:314-316: `logging_strategy: str = "steps"`, `logging_steps: float = 500`.

Same config with sampling_mode='poisson' (deterministic PLD) -> steps run 1 of 16, stop fired True. gaussian/poisson -> steps run 1 of 16, stop fired True.
docs/user-guide/huggingface/training-arguments.md:72-81 still describes the log-boundary contract only, so the per-step guarantee that #392 added is silently absent for MF defaults.
survivors.fix_sketch: Either (a) evaluate the accountant's epsilon on every accounted step whenever `ctx.stop_at_step is None` and a target is set (the MC PLD is cached per horizon-prefix, so the marginal cost is a cache hit within a band group), or (b) run the same binary search offline for MC accountants with a monotone-envelope guard and fall back to per-step evaluation only if the guard fails, or at minimum (c) refuse the configuration: raise when `privacy_target_epsilon` is set with a fixed multiplier, an MC sampler, and `logging_steps` larger than a safe bound.

survivors.title: DP-FTRL resume in calibrated mode silently changes sigma mid-horizon; the drift guard designed to stop exactly that is disabled for calibrated runs and the MF noise buffer mixes both scales
survivors.claim: `RuntimeCheckpoint.noise_multiplier` is tagged `drift='dp_relevant'` and `_warn_on_arg_drift` raises for DP-FTRL on that field ('the matrix-factorization strategy is computed for the original composition shape'). But `_current_values_for_drift` deliberately returns `None` for `noise_multiplier` when `ctx.calibration_source == 'calibrated'`, and the drift loop skips None -- so the one resume mode that *always* changes the multiplier is the one mode the guard never sees. The rebuilt `mf_gaussian_noise` closes over the NEW multiplier (`resolved_noise_multiplier` is a closure variable, not part of MFNoiseState), while `_apply_runtime_state` restores the old streaming-matrix state. Because `_streaming_mf_noise` scales the iid draw by `stddev` *before* pushing it into the streaming buffer, the released correlated noise for `bands` steps after the resume boundary is a mixture of sigma_old-scaled and sigma_new-scaled columns. No accountant models a sigma-heterogeneous MF release: the resume objective prices the suffix as a homogeneous sigma_new K-prefix of the same N-step strategy.
survivors.failure_scenario: mf_band (bands=4) + privacy_target_epsilon=3.0, max_steps=16, preempted after step 8 and resumed from checkpoint-8. Phase 1 calibrates nm=0.7670596313476563; phase 2 recalibrates nm=0.7667578125000001 over the remaining 8 steps and trains to completion with no exception and no warning. Steps 9..12 are emitted from a BandMF streaming buffer holding sigma_old-scaled draws for columns 5..8 and sigma_new-scaled draws for columns 9..12, so their per-coordinate scale is neither sigma_old nor sigma_new. When the recalibrated multiplier moves further (any preemption point that is not a band boundary, or a resume whose remaining budget differs materially), the post-boundary band is under- or over-noised relative to what both the prefix and the suffix PLD price.

(3) _mf_gaussian_noise.py:113 binds resolved_noise_multiplier as a closure variable and :166-172 derives base_stddev per call; it is not a field of MFNoiseState, so _apply_runtime_state (_dp_trainer.py:5204-5205) restores the old streaming buffer under a noise_fn built with the new sigma. (4) _engine.py:401-407 scales the iid draw by stddev BEFORE noising.multiply_next, so the buffer holds sigma-scaled columns. I reproduced the mixing directly (band_mf bands=4, N=8, fixed key, phase-1 nm=1.0 for 4 steps -> state_dict -> rebuilt at nm=3.0 -> from_state_dict): step-4 post/ref ratio [1.4854, 0.4956, 3.2754, 2.4275] instead of a constant 3.0. (5) I reproduced the trainer path end to end and established the DIRECTION the reporter left open. Resuming mf_band/poisson (bands=4, max_steps=16, target 3.0) at a band boundary (step 8) moves nm 0.7670596 -> 0.7667578 (0.04% down), but resuming at a NON-boundary step with the identical target moves it UP: step 5 -> ratio 1.0358, step 3 -> 1.0248. sigma_new > sigma_old means the first bands-1 steps after the boundary carry old smaller-sigma columns while the suffix accounting prices them at sigma_new — genuinely under-noised, the non-conservative direction. Worse, privacy_target_epsilon is never compared (absent from _current_values_for_drift), so resuming with a changed target is neither warned nor blocked: 3.0 -> 2.8 gives ratio 1.0909, unbounded in principle. Every run completed with no exception and an empty captured-warnings list. No test pins calibrated-resume behaviour. Severity kept high: a sigma-heterogeneous MF release that no accountant models, silent, on the flagship DP-FTRL resume path, in the under-noising direction for ordinary mid-run resumes, with the guard written for exactly this case bypassed. Not marked tracked: open #683 and closed #685 concern the accountant-side prefix PLD for horizon processes and its planned removal in #757; neither mentions the drift-guard bypass or the sigma-mixed streaming buffer, a mechanism-side defect that would survive #683's remediation.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A calibrated DP-FTRL run (target epsilon set, multiplier None) is preempted and resumed. _calibrate_noise recalibrates over the remaining steps against the saved prefix accountant, producing a different multiplier; _current_values_for_drift returns None for noise_multiplier in calibrated mode, so the DP-FTRL dp_relevant guard that would raise never sees it. mf_gaussian_noise is rebuilt closing over the NEW sigma while _apply_runtime_state restores the OLD streaming buffer whose columns were already scaled by the old sigma. For the next bands-1 steps the released correlated noise is a mixture of both scales — reproduced as a step-4 per-coordinate ratio of [1.4854, 0.4956, 3.2754, 2.4275] for a deliberate 3x switch. Measured on the real DPTrainer (mf_band, bands=4, poisson, max_steps=16, target 3.0), a resume at step 5 raises the multiplier 3.6% (0.76706 -> 0.79453) and at step 3 by 2.5%, so those boundary steps are ~2-3% under-noised relative to the sigma the suffix accounting charges; resuming with a lowered target (3.0 -> 2.8, never drift-checked) raises it 9.1%. All runs complete with no exception and no warning. No accountant prices a sigma-heterogeneous MF release; the resume objective prices the suffix as a homogeneous sigma_new prefix of the same N-step strategy.

survivors.title: Default privacy_target_delta documented as 1/(10*dataset_size) but computed as 1/dataset_size**1.1, a weaker delta at every realistic dataset size
survivors.claim: The training-arguments guide tells users the unset default is `1 / (10 * dataset_size)`. The trainer computes `1.0 / (dataset_size**1.1)`. Since n**1.1 < 10n for every n < 10**10, the delta actually used is always LARGER (weaker) than documented -- 2.5x at n=1e6, 6.6x at n=64. docs/reference/transformers.md:175 states the correct formula, so the two user-facing pages contradict each other on a privacy parameter.
survivors.failure_scenario: A user with a 1e6-example corpus leaves privacy_target_delta unset, reads training-arguments.md, and reports the run as (eps, 1e-7)-DP. The run actually calibrated and accounted at delta = 1/(1e6**1.1) = 2.51e-7 -- the published guarantee is a factor 2.5 stronger in delta than what was purchased. The reported epsilon is also the epsilon at the larger delta, so restating it at the documented delta is not conservative.
evidence: docs/user-guide/huggingface/training-arguments.md:45: `privacy_target_delta=1e-5,          # default: 1 / (10 * dataset_size)`
_dp_trainer.py:1481-1484: `target_delta = (a.privacy_target_delta if a.privacy_target_delta is not None else 1.0 / (dataset_size**1.1))`
docs/reference/transformers.md:175: '| `privacy_target_delta` | ... | Computed as `1 / dataset_size**1.1` when unset. |' -- contradicts the guide.
RUN (scratchpad/tc_warn.py, dataset_size=64, delta unset): every log row carries `'privacy_delta': '0.01031'` = 1/64**1.1, versus 1/(10*64) = 0.0015625 from the documented formula.
survivors.fix_sketch: Correct docs/user-guide/huggingface/training-arguments.md:45 to `1 / dataset_size**1.1` (matching docs/reference/transformers.md:175), and state explicitly that this exceeds 1/n for small n so users on small corpora must set the field.

survivors.title: acc.cached() on the DP-FTRL accountant is a warned no-op: a RuntimeWarning fires at every log boundary, every evaluation and on resume, and the intended amortization never happens
survivors.claim: For any MF mechanism the accountant's process contains a DpHorizonProcess (CachedProcess -> PerStep -> BMinSep/BallsInBins/CyclicPoisson), so `cached(Accountant)` takes the `_contains_horizon_process` branch in _cached.py:164-172, emits `RuntimeWarning('cached() skipped a whole-horizon prefix; cache its PerStep adapter before accumulation instead.')` and returns the accountant unchanged. The advice in the warning is already followed by the trainer (`step_process=acc.cached(mechanism(noise_multiplier))` at _dp_trainer.py:1598), so it is unactionable, and the epsilon query at the next line recomputes the whole-horizon PLD instead of reusing a cached boundary -- for b_min_sep / balls_in_bins that is a ~3M-sample Monte Carlo evaluation per log boundary.
survivors.failure_scenario: A DP-FTRL run with logging_steps=4 and 16 steps emits four identical RuntimeWarnings from library code with no user-actionable remedy; under `-W error` (or a stricter downstream warning filter) the training run aborts. Epsilon values remain correct, but the amortization the call site exists to provide is silently absent.
evidence: _cached.py:164-172 and 177-184: `case Accountant() if _contains_horizon_process(process.process): warnings.warn('cached() skipped a whole-horizon prefix; ...', RuntimeWarning); return process`.
_cached.py:191-209 `_contains_horizon_process` walks through CachedProcess / Composed / Repeated / PerStep, so the trainer's `Repeated(CachedProcess(PerStep(horizon)), k)` matches.
RUN (scratchpad/tc_warn.py, mf_band+poisson, 16 steps, logging_steps=4): `4 ('RuntimeWarning', 'cached() skipped a whole-horizon prefix; cache its PerStep adapter bef')`.

RUN (scratchpad/tc_agree.py): the missing cache does not change epsilon -- calibration objective, plain fold and fold+re-cache-every-10 are bit-for-bit identical for mf_band/poisson, mf_band/b_min_sep, mf_blt/balls_in_bins and mf_identity/poisson.
survivors.fix_sketch: Have the trainer skip `acc.cached(ctx.accounting)` when `ctx.mechanism_kind != 'gaussian'`, or make `cached()` return the accountant unchanged without warning when the horizon process is already behind a CachedProcess/PerStep boundary (the case the warning tells the caller to create).

verification.title: acc.cached() on the DP-FTRL accountant is a warned no-op: a RuntimeWarning fires at every log boundary, every evaluation and on resume, and the intended amortization never happens

The trainer calls acc.cached(ctx.accounting) at _dp_trainer.py:3959 (log boundary), 3244 (_after_evaluate) and 1144 (resume). Reproduced: mf_band + poisson, 16 steps, logging_steps=4 raises the warning 4 times. The advice is already followed at _dp_trainer.py:1598 (`step_process=acc.cached(mechanism(noise_multiplier))`, which takes the PerStep branch at _cached.py:176 without warning), so it is unactionable at the trainer's own call sites. Epsilon is unaffected — the accountant is returned intact and the PLD is recomputed. Two corrections: (a) the warning does fire on every call, but Python's default RuntimeWarning filter prints once per (message, category, module, lineno), so an ordinary run shows one message, not four — the count of 4 came from warnings.simplefilter('always'); (b) the -W error abort is real but requires opting into error-on-warning. survivors.title: DPTrainer.train() docstring and the HF training-arguments guide misdescribe resume drift and stop-at-epsilon cadence
survivors.claim: The train() docstring says 'Changing privacy_noise_multiplier / privacy_target_epsilon between checkpoint and resume warns but is allowed -- ... the warning guards against silent drift.' In reality: for DP-FTRL with a pinned multiplier the drift raises ValueError (_dp_trainer.py:5325-5332), and in calibrated mode the multiplier change is neither warned nor blocked (_dp_trainer.py:5393-5401 returns None). Separately, docs/user-guide/huggingface/training-arguments.md:72-81 still describes stop-at-epsilon as a check that 'runs every logging_steps', which is now true only for the Monte-Carlo samplers -- deterministic accountants check every accounted step via predict_stop_step.
survivors.failure_scenario: An operator resuming a DP-FTRL run with a recalibrated multiplier reads the docstring, expects a warning if anything privacy-relevant drifted, sees a clean log, and concludes the resumed run matches the accounted mechanism. Conversely a user reading the guide assumes the stop check is coarse and sets logging_steps=1 to tighten it, without realising that for MF defaults that is the only thing keeping the budget bounded (see the stop-at-epsilon finding).
evidence: _dp_trainer.py:932-939 docstring text quoted above.
_dp_trainer.py:5325-5332: `raise ValueError(f"DP-FTRL resume forbids drift on {f.name!r}: ...")`.
RUN (scratchpad/tc_resume_trainer.py, mf_band calibrated resume): nm changed 0.7670596313476563 -> 0.7667578125000001 and the captured warning list was empty.
RUN (same script, earlier variant that extended max_steps 8->16): `ValueError: DP-FTRL resume forbids drift on 'total_steps'` -- so the raise path is live, contradicting 'warns but is allowed'.

docs/user-guide/huggingface/training-arguments.md:78-79: 'The check runs every `logging_steps` (so setting `logging_steps=0` disables it silently ...)' vs _dp_trainer.py:1178-1194 predict_stop_step + 1873-1880 per-step integer check.
survivors.fix_sketch: Rewrite the train() resume paragraph to state the three actual dispositions (intentional_extend / shape warn / dp_relevant warn-for-DP-SGD, raise-for-DP-FTRL) and note that the calibrated multiplier is exempt. Update the stop-at-epsilon section to say the check is per accounted step for deterministic accountants and log-boundary-only for b_min_sep / balls_in_bins.

verification.title: DPTrainer.train() docstring and the HF training-arguments guide misdescribe resume drift and stop-at-epsilon cadence
verification.reasoning: Both misdescriptions verified against executed behaviour. The docstring at _dp_trainer.py:932-939 states without qualification that changing privacy_noise_multiplier / privacy_target_epsilon between checkpoint and resume 'warns but is allowed ... the warning guards against silent drift.' I ran all three cases. (a) DP-FTRL with a pinned multiplier 1.0 -> 2.0 raises ValueError: DP-FTRL resume forbids drift on 'noise_multiplier' (_dp_trainer.py:5325-5332) — not allowed, not a warning; the same drift on gaussian logs the documented warning. (b) DP-FTRL in calibrated mode changes the multiplier on every resume and neither warns nor raises, because _current_values_for_drift returns None for that field (5399-5407) — captured warnings empty across four resume variants. (c) privacy_target_epsilon is never compared at all: absent from the dict _current_values_for_drift returns, and I resumed with the target moved 3.0 -> 2.8 and 3.0 -> 4.0 with no warning in either case. survivors.title: Suite cannot detect a 2% divergence between applied and reported Gaussian noise (real epsilon +4.4% at DP-SGD defaults)
survivors.claim: Every empirical noise-magnitude assertion in the repository is a loose absolute-tolerance check on a single sample (|sigma_hat - target| < 0.05 at nm=1.0 over n=8192, < 0.1 at nm=2.5 over n=10000, < 0.1 at nm=3.0, < 0.05 at nm=2.0), i.e. 2.5%-5% relative slack against a sampling error of ~0.8%. Nothing binds the realized noise to the reported `NoisedPytree.noise_stddev` any tighter. I mutated `opaque.api.dpsgd.noise._gaussian` so the applied noise is a constant factor below the reported `noise_stddev` (the exact shape of a silent privacy loss: accountant charges sigma, sampler draws k*sigma) and bisected the detection floor. At 0.90x, 8 tests fail. At 0.97x, only `test_bounded_gaussian.py::TestBoundedGaussian::test_noise_distribution_truncnorm` fails, and it fails on a fixed-seed KS p-value (0.0024), not by design. At 0.98x the entire opaque-dpsgd suite passes (719 passed, 0 failed) and so do tests/integration + opaque-transformers (990 passed, 0 failed). This is a coverage gap, not a live bug: the shipped code is correct today. But a 2% understatement is worth +4.4% on the real epsilon and CI would be green.
survivors.failure_scenario: A future refactor of `_sample` / `_clipped_stddev` / the compute-dtype cast path introduces a systematic <=2% shortfall between the noise actually drawn and the `noise_stddev` the accountant is charged for (e.g. an fp32<->bf16 round-trip, a Bessel-correction slip, a per-group `effective` bound recomputed slightly low). Users train at reported nm=1.0, q=0.01, 1000 steps and are told eps=1.8282; the mechanism they actually ran is nm=0.98, whose eps is 1.9082 (+4.37%). The full PR gate, the main gate, and the integration suite all pass.
evidence: Mutation harness (repo left read-only; package src copied to a scratch dir and shadowed via PYTHONPATH): in the copy of packages/opaque-dpsgd/src/opaque/api/dpsgd/noise/_gaussian.py the two `_sample` call sites (line 307 `noised_leaves.append(_sample(tensor, group_std, generator))` and line 310 `return tree_map(lambda t: _sample(t, effective_stddev, generator), grads)`) were changed to scale the std by k while `_clipped_stddev` (line 312-324) still reports the unscaled value.

k=0.90: `uv run pytest packages/opaque-dpsgd/tests tests/integration -m 'not cuda and not mps and not slow and not distributed'` -> 8 failed, 876 passed. Failing: test_gaussian_compute_dtype.py::test_observed_variance_matches_calibrated_stddev, ::test_bf16_observed_variance_matches_calibrated_stddev, ::test_bf16_default_compute_dtype_beats_native_bf16, test_noise.py::TestGaussian::{test_noise_stddev,test_noise_normality,test_clipped_input_returns_noisy_pytree}, test_bounded_gaussian.py::TestBoundedGaussian::test_noise_distribution_truncnorm, ddp/test_gaussian_noise.py::TestNoiseCalibration::test_noise_std_matches_stddev_roughly.
k=0.97: packages/opaque-dpsgd/tests -> 1 failed, 718 passed. Only failure is test_bounded_gaussian.py:182 'KS test failed with p=0.0023593767546117306'.
k=0.98: packages/opaque-dpsgd/tests -> '719 passed, 2 skipped, 126 deselected'. tests/integration + packages/opaque-transformers/tests -> '990 passed, 16 skipped, 102 deselected'. Zero failures.

Epsilon cost, computed with the shipped accountant: `(dpsgd_acc.poisson(dpsgd_acc.gaussian(nm), 0.01) * 1000).epsilon_at(1e-5)` gives nm=1.00 -> 1.8282, nm=0.98 -> 1.9082 (+4.37%), nm=0.97 -> 1.9510 (+6.72%), nm=0.95 -> 2.0429 (+11.7%).

Tolerance sources: test_gaussian_compute_dtype.py:32 `assert abs(observed_std - 1.0) < 0.05` (n=8192 -> sampling sd of sigma_hat ~ 0.0078, so the gate is ~6.4 sigma); test_noise.py:113 `assert abs(measured_stddev - target_stddev) < 0.1` with target 2.5 (4.0% relative); test_noise.py:166 `assert abs(output.pytree.std().item() - 3.0) < 0.1` (3.3% relative).

packages/opaque-dpftrl/tests/noise/test_realized_stddev.py checks the *reported* metadata against the analytic row-L2 at rel=1e-9..1e-12 (lines 88, 145-146, 169, 188, 205-208, 225) but never measures the drawn samples, so it does not close this gap for the MF path either.
survivors.fix_sketch: Add one high-n statistical conformance test per noise mechanism that ties the realized second moment to the reported `noise_stddev` at a tolerance derived from the sample size rather than a round number: draw >=10^6 coordinates, assert `abs(sigma_hat/output.noise_stddev - 1) < 5/sqrt(2*n)` (~0.35% at n=10^6, still a 5-sigma gate) for gaussian_noise, per-group gaussian_noise, and mf_gaussian_noise. Mark it `slow` if needed but keep it in the main gate. Optionally add a chi-square test on sum(x^2)/(n*sigma^2), which is more powerful than KS against a pure scale error.

verification.title: Suite cannot detect a 2% divergence between applied and reported Gaussian noise (real epsilon +4.4% at DP-SGD defaults)
verification.reasoning: I did not re-run the reporter's full mutation sweep; I settled the detection floor analytically and numerically instead, which is stronger. I enumerated every empirical noise-magnitude assertion in the repo (grep for .std() across packages/*/tests and tests/): test_gaussian_compute_dtype.py:32/40/57, test_noise.py:113/166, ddp/test_gaussian_noise.py:207, dpsgd_ddp_helpers.py:566/572, and the tightest, validation/test_dp_guarantees.py:437 (pytest.approx(nm*C, rel=5e-2) at n=200_000). Then I computed each test's realized statistic at its own fixed seed and solved for the smallest uniform scale factor k on the applied noise that still passes: compute_dtype fp32 k>=0.9503, compute_dtype bf16 k>=0.9503, bf16-beats-native k>=0.9682, test_noise stddev k>=0.9450, clipped_input k>=0.9516, dp_guarantees realized k>=0.9466. Sampling error is <=0.8% at these n, so the slack is genuine, not statistically necessary. Real, verified coverage gap that directly contradicts the acceptance criteria of #348 ('A deliberate scale or sensitivity mismatch makes the suite fail'), closed as completed on 2026-08-27 — an incomplete-fix report against a closed issue, not a duplicate of anything open (#666 covers Monte Carlo regression vectors for balls_in_bins/b_min_sep, a different path). Severity lowered to low and affects_epsilon corrected to false: the reporter states the shipped code is correct today, I found no live mismatch, and no epsilon computed by the current tree is wrong. survivors.title: The only epsilon-value regression test for the CachedProcess repeated_pld bug (OPQ-005) was deleted; the surviving guards use the one strategy where the buggy and correct answers are bit-identical
survivors.claim: Commit 009975cd (#290) fixed OPQ-005 and shipped `TestCachedPerStepRepeatedPld` in packages/opaque-dpftrl/tests/accounting/test_per_step.py, whose docstring explicitly said band-MF with bands>1 'is required so the Identity degeneracy (where K-fold single-step composition happens to match the horizon PLD) cannot mask a missing CachedProcess.repeated_pld relay'. Commit 819ef0d9 (#679) deleted that whole class, including `test_cached_repeated_pld_is_horizon_not_self_compose`, and replaced it with `test_cached_horizon_step_preserves_prefix`, which uses `identity_strategy()` - exactly the degeneracy the deleted docstring warned about - and asserts Python object identity (`is`) rather than any epsilon value. The suite does still fail if the relay is removed, but only through those `is` assertions; not one numeric assertion anywhere discriminates. Relaxing `is` to `==` in either surviving test (a natural 'fix' if the identity assertion ever gets flaky under a cache change) silently removes all coverage for a ~2.2x epsilon inflation on every band-MF run.

survivors.title: CI test-package matrix is a hand-maintained inventory with no coverage guard, after the auto-discovery script was deleted - and pyproject.toml still documents automatic pickup
survivors.claim: `.github/workflows/python-tests.yml` enumerates the packages to test as five hardcoded `suite.paths` blocks. Nothing in the repository checks that this list covers `packages/*`. The repo previously had exactly this guard - `.github/scripts/discover_package_matrices.py` was added by 5b2a2957 (#464) on 2026-08-03 - and it was deleted by 938a8a56 (#676) on 2026-08-20, with 9431203c (#704) then collapsing the per-package steps into the current static matrix. New packages, renames, and deletes don't need matching edits in CI. ... Identical behavior locally (`pytest` from repo root) and in CI.' That is now false for CI, and it is the sentence a contributor adding a package will read.
survivors.failure_scenario: A contributor adds `packages/opaque-<new>/` with a full `tests/` tree (as happened for opaque-alignment during this delta) and does not edit `.github/workflows/python-tests.yml`. survivors.title: allow-empty-test-selection makes the distributed and CUDA lanes pass on zero collected tests, and two of five distributed suites already rely on that escape hatch

survivors.title: A test that creates a real Gloo process group and binds a port runs in the parallel lane, and fail-opens with a silent skip when it finds one already live
survivors.claim: `test_dpo_brings_up_the_process_group_before_precomputing` is the only test that pins the DPO reference-forward ordering contract (the reference forward must find a live process group, or it cannot shard). It is marked `@pytest.mark.slow` but NOT `@pytest.mark.distributed`, so it does not go to the serial distributed lane; it runs in the main-branch 'Linux amd64 (locked)' lane whose marker is `not cuda and not mps and not distributed` under `-n auto --dist loadscope`. Inside, it brings up a real 1-rank Gloo group on a port obtained by bind-then-close (`with socket.socket() as sock: sock.bind(...); port = sock.getsockname()[1]`, then used ~20 lines later), i.e. a classic TOCTOU against the sibling xdist workers on the same host. It also guards itself with `if torch.distributed.is_initialized(): pytest.skip(...)`, which converts contamination into a silent pass rather than a failure - the author evidently anticipated the leak.
survivors.failure_scenario: On a main-branch run, the port reserved at line 1943 is taken between the `with` block closing the socket and `real_init` connecting - by another xdist worker in the same job, or by `find_free_port()` in tests/_support/opaque_test_support.py:78-82 (same bind-then-close shape) - and the test fails or hangs to the 40-minute job timeout. In the other direction, if any test scheduled earlier in the same worker leaves a group initialized, the `is_initialized()` guard skips this test entirely and the DPO ordering contract goes unverified with a green run; because `--dist loadscope` assignment depends on `-n auto` (runner CPU count), which tests share a worker is not stable across runners.
evidence: packages/opaque-transformers/tests/opaque_transformers/test_trl_trainers.py:1914 `@pytest.mark.slow` with no `distributed` marker, contrasted with every other real-process-group test: packages/opaque-dpsgd/tests/ddp/test_dpsgd_cpu_gloo.py:16, packages/opaque-dpftrl/tests/ddp/test_dpftrl_cpu_gloo.py:15, packages/opaque-engine/tests/ddp/test_cpu_gloo.py:9 all use `pytestmark = pytest.mark.distributed`, and packages/opaque-engine/tests/ddp/test_second_moment_reduce.py:51-64 pairs `slow` with `distributed` on each test.

Lane markers: .github/workflows/ci.yml:35 'not cuda and not mps and not distributed' with .github/workflows/ci.yml:36 'pytest-xdist: -n auto --dist loadscope'; the distributed lane (ci.yml:41-49) passes no xdist input at all, i.e. serial.
Lines 1942-1944 reserve the port and release it before use; `real_init(backend='gloo', init_method=f'tcp://127.0.0.1:{port}', world_size=1, rank=0)` at 1955-1960 is the consumer.
Line 1935-1936: `if torch.distributed.is_initialized(): pytest.skip('a process group is already live in this worker')`.
survivors.fix_sketch: Add `@pytest.mark.distributed` so it lands in the serial lane alongside the other real-process-group tests, and replace the `is_initialized()` skip with a fixture that asserts no group is live at setup and destroys any leftover at teardown (a leaked group is a bug in whichever test leaked it, not a reason to stop testing this one).

verification.title: A test that creates a real Gloo process group and binds a port runs in the parallel lane, and fail-opens with a silent skip when it finds one already live
verification.reasoning: Every structural claim checks out: packages/opaque-transformers/tests/opaque_transformers/test_trl_trainers.py:1914 carries only `@pytest.mark.slow`, unlike every other real-process-group test (packages/opaque-dpsgd/tests/ddp/test_dpsgd_cpu_gloo.py, packages/opaque-dpftrl/tests/ddp/test_dpftrl_cpu_gloo.py, packages/opaque-engine/tests/ddp/test_cpu_gloo.py all set `pytestmark = pytest.mark.distributed`); it therefore lands in the main-branch lane at ci.yml:30-40 (`not cuda and not mps and not distributed`, `-n auto --dist loadscope`) rather than the serial distributed lane (ci.yml:41-49, no xdist input). Lines 1942-1944 do bind-then-close to reserve a port that real_init consumes ~15 lines later, and lines 1934-1936 skip on `torch.distributed.is_initialized()`. What I could not establish is any trigger for either failure mode. The only other bind-then-close helper, tests/_support/opaque_test_support.py:80-85, is used exclusively by `distributed`-marked tests that never co-run in this lane; the ephemeral-port window is milliseconds against a ~28k-port range.
