Not established: any concrete trigger. No other in-process group initializer runs in that lane (the DDP-trainer tests spawn subprocesses and are `distributed`-marked), so the skip guard is currently inert, and the port race window is a few milliseconds against the ephemeral range. survivors.title: New patched-vs-upstream parity suite silently pytest.skips gradient and vmap-grad parity for 4 of 26 registered model families, on the grounds that the patches change the backward Jacobian
survivors.claim: This is a delta on open issue #330 ('Establish patched-versus-upstream numerical parity'), not a duplicate of it. The suite that issue asks for now exists (added by 5936552b, #481, during this delta) and reports green - but it exempts gpt2, qwen3_next, deepseek_v4 and gpt_oss from both `test_backward_grads_parity` and `test_vmap_grad_parity` via bare `pytest.skip`, and additionally exempts deepseek_v4/gpt_oss/qwen3_next from `test_forward_logits_parity`. The stated reasons are not environmental: they say the shipped patches change behavior ('kv_cache/batchify patches alter backward graph', 'runtime compatibility shims change sink gradients'). `test_vmap_grad_parity` is the DP-relevant one - vmap(grad(...)) is exactly how per-record gradients reach `clipped_grad` - so for these four registered families the per-example gradients Opaque clips are of unverified fidelity, and the coverage-guard test `test_parity_families_covered` does not account for the grad-parity exemptions (it subtracts only `_PARITY_SKIP_FAMILIES`, a different, one-element set). Using `skip` rather than `xfail(strict=True)` also means the suite will never tell anyone when a family starts passing.
survivors.failure_scenario: A user fine-tunes a gpt_oss or deepseek_v4 model with DPTrainer. `apply_model_patches` installs shims that the repository's own test comments say change the backward Jacobian; the resulting per-record gradients differ from the model's true gradients. Clipping still bounds sensitivity, so the privacy accounting stays valid, but training silently optimizes a different objective and the parity suite is green because those families are skipped by name.
evidence: packages/opaque-patches/tests/transformers/models/test_parity.py:85-93: `# Families whose gradient parity is unreliable due to custom autograd / # functions in the patches that change the backward Jacobian path even / # when the forward is bit-identical.` then `_GRAD_PARITY_SKIP_FAMILIES = {'gpt2', 'qwen3_next', 'deepseek_v4', 'gpt_oss'}`.
Line 269-270 in `test_backward_grads_parity` and line 456-457 in `test_vmap_grad_parity`: `if family in _GRAD_PARITY_SKIP_FAMILIES: pytest.skip(f'{family} has unreliable gradient parity')`.

`uv run python -c 'from opaque.api.patches.transformers import supported_families; print(sorted(supported_families()))'` -> 26 families including deepseek_v4, gpt2, gpt_oss, qwen3_next, i.e. all four are registered and will be patched at runtime.

Coverage guard at line 482-490 computes `families = set(supported_families()) - _PARITY_SKIP_FAMILIES` where `_PARITY_SKIP_FAMILIES = {'qwen3_5_moe'}` (line 73-75) - it does not notice the grad-parity exemptions.
`git log --oneline 79c916e3..4b13d82 -S'_GRAD_PARITY_SKIP_FAMILIES'` -> 5936552b only, i.e. the exemptions shipped with the suite.
survivors.fix_sketch: Convert each entry to `pytest.param(family, marks=pytest.mark.xfail(strict=True, reason=...))` so the suite reports when a family starts passing and cannot rot into a permanent hole, and either de-register the four families from `supported_families()` or document them in docs/user-guide/huggingface.md as not gradient-verified. Extend `test_parity_families_covered` to also assert that every grad-parity exemption is listed in a single reviewed constant with an issue reference.

survivors.title: Test comment asserts a PLD cross-test cache-contamination hazard that the current cache implementation does not have
survivors.claim: `test_per_call_matches_global_config` carries the comment '``pld_at``'s lru_cache keys on (process, kwargs), not the resolved global config: the no-kwargs entry for an equal-valued process must not have been populated under a different global config by an earlier test (all files pin the same _MC_KW).' That was true before #675/#679; it is false at 4b13d82. Both `pld_cache` and `horizon_pld_cache` now build the key as `(resolved DiscretizationConfig, self._pld_cache_key(...), n_steps)`, so a differently-configured global cannot alias. The comment matters because it describes a cross-test contamination hazard as live and pins an implicit convention ('all files pin the same _MC_KW') that is already violated - packages/opaque-dpftrl/tests/accounting/test_b_min_sep.py:230-234 sets `mc_resolution=5e-2, mc_failure_probability=1e-2, seed=3`, a different config from `_MC_KW`.
survivors.failure_scenario: A maintainer investigating a PLD-cache issue reads this comment, concludes the cache is not config-keyed, and either adds redundant `cache_clear()` calls (which wipe the shared entries other tests' `is` assertions depend on) or re-derives the key to 'fix' a hazard that no longer exists. Conversely, someone tightening the cache key may treat the comment as a spec and preserve a non-existent constraint.
evidence: packages/opaque-accounting/src/opaque/api/accounting/core/_pld_cache.py:178-186 (pld_cache): `config = _resolve_config(...)` then `cache.get_or_compute(self, (config, self._pld_cache_key(), None), ...)`; :231-243 (horizon_pld_cache): `cache.get_or_compute(self, (config, self._pld_cache_key(n_steps=n_steps), n_steps), ...)`. `_CacheKey = tuple[DiscretizationConfig, Hashable, int | None]` at line 21.
`DiscretizationConfig` is `@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)` (discretization.py:17-18), so it hashes and compares by value - two different global configs give two different keys.
packages/opaque-dpftrl/tests/accounting/test_b_min_sep.py:230-234 uses a config that is not `_MC_KW`, contradicting the comment's parenthetical.
The commit that made the comment obsolete is 493a9f4a 'fix(accounting): key PLD caches by resolved inputs (#675)', extended by 819ef0d9 (#679).
survivors.fix_sketch: Replace the comment with the fact it is now testing: the resolved config is part of the cache key, so `proc.epsilon_at(d, **mc)` and `set_discretization(**mc); proc.epsilon_at(d)` resolve to the same key and therefore the same Pld object. Consider asserting object identity in addition to value equality, which would make the test guard the keying property directly.

verification.title: Test comment asserts a PLD cross-test cache-contamination hazard that the current cache implementation does not have
verification.reasoning: Read both sides myself. packages/opaque-dpftrl/tests/accounting/test_per_step.py:414-418 carries the comment claiming the lru_cache 'keys on (process, kwargs), not the resolved global config'. That is false at 4b13d82: packages/opaque-accounting/src/opaque/api/accounting/core/_pld_cache.py declares `_CacheKey = tuple[DiscretizationConfig, Hashable, int | None]` (line 21), and both decorators call `_resolve_config(...)` first and then key on it -- `pld_cache` uses `(config, self._pld_cache_key(), None)` (lines ~178-186) and `horizon_pld_cache` uses `(config, self._pld_cache_key(n_steps=n_steps), n_steps)` (lines ~231-243). DiscretizationConfig is `@dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True)` (discretization.py:17-18), so it hashes and compares by value and two differently-valued globals cannot alias onto one entry. The comment's parenthetical convention is also already violated: packages/opaque-dpftrl/tests/accounting/test_b_min_sep.py:228-234 calls `acc.set_discretization(mc_resolution=5e-2, mc_failure_probability=1e-2, seed=3)`, which is not `_MC_KW`. No open tracked issue covers this. Severity low and non-epsilon: it is a stale explanatory comment in a test; the test itself still asserts the right thing and passes.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A maintainer debugging PLD caching reads the comment at test_per_step.py:414-418, believes the cache is not keyed by the resolved DiscretizationConfig, and either sprinkles defensive `cache_clear()` calls (evicting shared entries that other tests' identity assertions rely on) or 'preserves' the stated cross-file `_MC_KW` convention when tightening the key -- a constraint that test_b_min_sep.py already breaks and that the value-keyed cache made unnecessary at 493a9f4a/819ef0d9.

survivors.title: Quickstart and the DP-SGD tutorial publish a Poisson-amplified epsilon for a torch.randperm shuffled fixed-batch loop (published output says epsilon=3.00; honest bound >=18.85)
survivors.line: quickstart.md:44-51 and :79-91; dp_sgd_training.ipynb cell 9 and cell 13
survivors.claim: The two flagship onboarding walkthroughs calibrate the noise multiplier against `dpsgd_acc.poisson(dpsgd_acc.gaussian(nm), sample_rate) * total_steps` and then report that epsilon, but the training loop they ship draws batches with `torch.randperm` + contiguous slicing -- a deterministic shuffled partition, not Poisson subsampling. Poisson amplification does not apply, so the printed epsilon is not a valid guarantee.
survivors.failure_scenario: A user follows the Quick Start (the first runnable example in the docs) or the DP-SGD tutorial and ships a model believing epsilon=3.0. dp_sgd_training.ipynb (n=2000, batch=64, 20 epochs, 620 steps) calibrates nm=1.35683 and its COMMITTED cell output prints `Final privacy: (epsilon=3.00, delta=1e-05)`; mkdocs.yml:59-61 sets `execute: false`, so that exact number is what the published page shows. The deployed sampling gives each record exactly one participation per epoch with no subsampling randomness. The most generous honest accounting -- one unamplified Gaussian release per epoch, composed 20 times -- is (D.gaussian(1.35683)*20).epsilon_at(1e-5) = 18.850, a 6.3x understatement. Reading each of the 620 steps as an unamplified release gives 245.757 (82x). The quickstart (n=1000, batch=32, 10 epochs) is the same defect: calibrated nm=1.10530, printed epsilon ~3.05, honest per-epoch composition = 15.685 (5.2x) and per-step 199.103 (66x). verification.title: Quickstart and the DP-SGD tutorial publish a Poisson-amplified epsilon for a torch.randperm shuffled fixed-batch loop
verification.reasoning: The structural claim reproduces exactly; the quantitative claim does not, and I corrected it down. Confirmed: docs/getting-started/quickstart.md:44-51 calibrates against `dpsgd_acc.poisson(dpsgd_acc.gaussian(nm), sample_rate) * num_steps` and lines 79-91 then train with `torch.randperm` + contiguous slicing and print the Poisson epsilon; dp_sgd_training.ipynb cells 9 and 13 do the same and ship a committed output 'Final privacy: (epsilon=3.00, delta=1e-05)', with mkdocs.yml:59-61 setting `execute: false` so that literal number is published. Neither file contains PoissonSampler or DataLoader (grepped both). Poisson amplification genuinely does not apply to a shuffled equal-size partition, so the published figure has no applicable theorem behind it -- and closed issue #356's acceptance criterion ('every documented loop uses the sampler through a DataLoader and executes exactly the calibrated horizon') is unmet, so this is not tracked work. REFUTED, however, is the magnitude: the reporter's 'most generous honest accounting' ignores allocation-style amplification, which Opaque itself ships. Measured with the repo venv at the reporter's own calibrated nm=1.35682832673192: `random_allocation(gaussian(nm), num_bins=32, n_steps=32)` composed over 20 epochs = 2.830 (num_bins=31 variant: 2.880), versus the published 3.000 -- i.e. the closest applicable model gives a number BELOW what the docs print, not 6.3x above. Quickstart likewise: nm=1.105301145464182, RA(32 bins) x 10 epochs = 2.703 vs printed 3.046. So the claimed 18.85 / 245.76 / 199.10 'honest bounds' are not honest bounds; they are what you get by discarding all amplification. The residual real defects are (i) the published epsilon rests on the wrong subsampling theorem, and (ii) a genuine step-count under-count -- both loops execute one extra partial batch per epoch (32 releases against 31 accounted), so the tutorial makes 640 releases while accounting 620 (poisson*640 = 3.051 vs 3.000) and the quickstart executes 320 while calibrating 310. Note also that Opaque's random_allocation models independent balls-and-bins assignment (Feldman & Shenfeld 2026; Chua et al. 2025) while randperm gives an exactly-equal-size shuffle partition, so strictly neither shipped accountant is a proven bound for the deployed loop -- which is the point, but the gap is a few percent, not a factor of six. Severity demoted high -> medium accordingly: an unsupported-theorem claim in flagship onboarding docs, not a user shipping a wildly wrong epsilon.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A user follows the Quick Start or dp_sgd_training.ipynb and reports epsilon=3.00 for their model. The loop draws batches by `torch.randperm` + contiguous slicing -- a shuffled equal-size partition -- while the number was calibrated and reported under `dpsgd_acc.poisson(...)`, whose subsampling theorem does not apply to that sampler, and neither doc constructs a sampler at all. The published figure is therefore not backed by an applicable amplification result. Separately and independently, both loops execute one more optimizer step per epoch than they account for (32 batches vs `n_samples // batch_size` = 31), so the tutorial charges 620 releases for 640 executed (3.000 charged vs 3.051) and the quickstart charges 310 for 320 (3.046 printed against a 3.0 budget). The magnitude of the theorem mismatch is small, not large: recomputing at the same noise multiplier under Opaque's own `random_allocation` accountant -- the closest shipped model for shuffled fixed-size batching -- gives 2.830 for the tutorial and 2.703 for the quickstart, i.e. at or below the published numbers.

The trainer's documented mf_band + poisson pairing instead constructs a plain `opaque.dpsgd.sampling.PoissonSampler` over the full dataset (no bands, no separation) while accounting through the same CyclicPoisson group decomposition. verification.title: Trainer docs advertise mf_band + sampling_mode='poisson' while the runtime builds a plain PoissonSampler against the cyclic-group CyclicPoisson accountant
verification.reasoning: Verified every link, including by execution. (1) docs/user-guide/huggingface/training-arguments.md:142 lists '| mf_band | b_min_sep (or explicit poisson) | {"bands": 16} |' with no caveat. (2) _training_arguments.py:181-193 allow-lists `mf_band -> {b_min_sep, poisson}` with the in-code comment calling poisson 'a looser-but-valid alternative'. (3) _dpftrl.py:224-232 `build_sampler` for sampling_mode='poisson' returns `PoissonSampler(dataset, sample_rate=..., n_steps=..., ...)` from opaque.dpsgd.sampling -- no bands, no separation, independent draws every step. (4) _dpftrl.py:138-152 `build_amplifier_factory` for the same mode returns `_ftrl_poisson(mf_gaussian(nm, strategy), ...)` = CyclicPoisson, whose `pld_at` (_poisson.py:178-215) composes only `num_groups = ceil(rounded / bands)` per-group Poisson-Gaussian PLDs at `effective_nm = nm / sensitivity`. (5) `BandMfStrategy.sensitivity` is participation-blind -- I measured 0.9999999999999999 for (min_sep=1, max_participations=1000), (10, 100) and (1, 1) alike -- so nothing rescales the noise to pay for lost separation. (6) CyclicPoisson.min_sep is hardcoded to 1 with a comment admitting 'Cyclic Poisson provides no worst-case separation guarantee'. The b-group factorization in Choquette-Choo et al. (2023) is licensed by b-min-separated (cyclic) participation, under which a record's columns in the b-banded C have disjoint support so the run factors into ceil(n/b) independent one-participation Gaussians; plain Poisson gives min_sep=1, allows up to b participations inside one band block with overlapping columns, and the factorization is simply unsound -- the code charges one subsampled participation per b steps at sensitivity 1. Empirically the undercharge shows up as `poisson(mf_gaussian(1.0, band_mf_strategy(bands=10)), sample_rate=0.01, n_steps=1000).epsilon_at(1e-5) = 0.7180` versus 1.8282 for the identity strategy under the identical deployed sampler -- the full factor-b composition saving is claimed without the separation that earns it. The in-code 'looser-but-valid' comment is wrong in the unsafe direction. Worst of all, the matching sampler exists and is wired: _dpftrl.py:282-294 has a working `cyclic_poisson` branch building `CyclicPoissonSampler(dataset, sample_rate, bands=mf.strategy.bands, ...)`, and band-mf.md:295 tells users to 'Pair with CyclicPoissonSampler' -- but I confirmed by running TrainingArguments that mf_band + 'cyclic_poisson' is rejected ('allowed: [b_min_sep, poisson]') while mf_band + 'poisson' is accepted. So the allow-list admits precisely the wrong one of the two. Not a duplicate: open #359 concerns BandMfStrategy.sensitivity() semantics and paired second moments inside opaque-accounting/opaque-dpftrl; this is a trainer wiring + docs defect in opaque-transformers with its own one-line fix (swap 'poisson' for 'cyclic_poisson' in the mf_band allow-list, or reject it), and it is not among #319's sub-issues (347/353/355/359/360/361/362). Severity high, epsilon-affecting, unsafe direction.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A user sets TrainingArguments(privacy_noise_mechanism='mf_band', sampling_mode='poisson') -- presented at training-arguments.md:142 as a supported alternative with no warning, and accepted by the allow-list. build_sampler hands training a plain opaque.dpsgd.sampling.PoissonSampler over the whole dataset (independent per-step draws, min_sep=1, a record can appear in consecutive steps), while build_amplifier_factory prices the run through CyclicPoisson, which composes only ceil(n_steps/bands) per-group Poisson-Gaussian PLDs at effective_nm = nm/1.0. The ceil(n/b) group factorization is licensed only by b-min-separated participation; the deployed sampler provides none, and BandMfStrategy.sensitivity returns 1.0 regardless of min_sep or max_participations, so nothing compensates. The reported epsilon is materially undercharged -- at nm=1.0, q=0.01, n_steps=1000, bands=10 it reads 0.7180 while the same sampler under independent (identity) noise already costs 1.8282. Meanwhile CyclicPoissonSampler, the sampler that actually matches this accountant and that band-mf.md:295 instructs users to pair with, is built by build_sampler but rejected by the mf_band allow-list.

survivors.title: DPTrainer blesses mf_band + sampling_mode="poisson", which pairs the BandMF cyclic-Poisson accountant with a plain full-dataset PoissonSampler — violating the hypothesis of the cited Choquette-Choo et al. Theorem 4
survivors.claim: `_ALLOWED_SAMPLERS["mf_band"] = frozenset({"b_min_sep", "poisson"})` (_training_arguments.py:188) with the comment at :182-184 "``mf_band`` accepts ``\"poisson\"`` as a looser-but-valid alternative to its canonical ``\"b_min_sep\"`` participation pattern". Under that setting `build_amplifier_factory(sampling_mode="poisson", strategy=BandMfStrategy(bands=b))` returns `ftrl_acc.poisson(mf_gaussian(nm, BandMfStrategy), ...)` = `CyclicPoisson`, whose `pld_at` composes only `num_groups = ceil(n_steps/bands)` per-group Poisson-Gaussian PLDs at `effective_nm = nm / ||coef|| = nm / 1.0` (_poisson.py:178-188), while `build_sampler(sampling_mode="poisson", ...)` returns the DP-SGD `PoissonSampler` over the WHOLE dataset every step (_dpftrl.py:224-233, imported from `opaque.dpsgd.sampling` at :46-50) — `bands` is never passed. The accounting module cites this analysis to "BandMF amplification: Choquette-Choo et al. (2023) https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.08153" (_poisson.py:16). That paper's Theorem 4 reads: "Suppose C is b-banded and lower triangular, and the examples participating in each step are chosen according to Algorithm 2. Then BandMF satisfies any standard DP guarantee satisfied by performing k sensitivity-kappa queries on a dataset of size m-check = floor(m/b) using the Gaussian mechanism" — Algorithm 2 being the cyclic partition "D_1,...,D_b <- arbitrary partition of D. for i=1..n do j = i (mod b). S_i <- random size B subset of D_j." A plain full-dataset Poisson sampler is not Algorithm 2 (nor its Appendix-F generalisation): an example is eligible on EVERY round, so its participations are not b-separated and its contributions land in overlapping row-blocks of the b-banded C. The decomposition into ceil(n/b) independent subsampled Gaussians that CyclicPoisson.pld_at performs therefore has no proof behind it in this configuration, and the reported epsilon is not an upper bound. Additionally, `build_sampler`'s own docstring at :217-220 asserts the opposite of what it does: "Privacy-derived sampler parameters (``bands``, paper-``p``) are read off the built ``mf`` recipe / amplifier ... so the runtime sampler cannot desync from the accountant."
survivors.failure_scenario: `DPTrainingArguments(privacy_noise_mechanism="mf_band", sampling_mode="poisson", privacy_noise_mechanism_kwargs={"bands": 10}, train_batch_size=256, ...)` on a 50k-row dataset for 1000 steps. Validation accepts it (_training_arguments.py:1048). Measured on the current tree: `build_amplifier_factory(sampling_mode='poisson', strategy=band_mf_strategy(bands=10), sample_rate=256/50000, n_steps=1000)(1.0)` returns `CyclicPoisson` with `num_groups=100` and reports `epsilon_at(1e-5) = 0.355`; `build_sampler(sampling_mode='poisson', ...)` returns `PoissonSampler` with no `bands` attribute. Iterating that sampler for 1000 steps gives 206,254 consecutive-participation gaps of which 5.6% are smaller than `bands=10` and the minimum gap is 1 — the b-min-separation the accountant assumes is violated on 1 in 18 participation pairs. The sensitivity the accountant divides by is `BandMfStrategy.sensitivity(...) = ||coef|| = 1.0000` (which ignores its `min_sep`/`max_participations` arguments entirely, _band_mf.py:126-128), whereas the true sensitivity of the same 10-banded Toeplitz C under min_sep=1 is 1.92 at k=2, 4.47 at k=5, 7.97 at k=10 and 11.82 at k=18 (18 was the largest participation count actually observed). The deployed noise is calibrated against a sensitivity up to ~12x too small, and only 100 of the 1000 rounds are composed.

Plain Poisson breaks it two ways I quantified: per band-block of 10 rounds a record is eligible 10 times, so its per-group participation probability is 1-(1-q)^10 = 0.0500 vs the charged q = 0.00512 (composing the same 100 groups at 0.0500 gives eps 3.505 vs 0.355, ~10x); and participations inside one block overlap, so the true min-sep-1 sensitivity of the same 10-banded C is 1.921 at k=2, 7.967 at k=10, 11.82 at k=18 (_native.toeplitz_minsep_sensitivity_squared) against the charged 1.0. No runtime warning; _dpftrl.py:217-220 claims the opposite. Not a duplicate: #320 and its sub-issue #356 (sampler-accounting contract) were both CLOSED as completed on 2026-08-27 while this pairing still ships and is test-pinned; open #359 covers only BandMfStrategy sensitivity semantics, not the sampler/amplifier pairing, and the fix here is independent (drop 'poisson' from mf_band's allow-list or route it to CyclicPoissonSampler).

survivors.title: Truncated-Poisson accounting silently switches the adjacency relation to Ganesh's dataset-size-dependent add-or-remove-1-of-n, and its sole citation is the unresolvable key [Gan25]
survivors.claim: The truncated-Poisson PLD is documented as `Uses the mixture formula from \[Gan25\]` (:20) and `Hockey-stick divergence for truncated Poisson (mixture formula from \[Gan25\])` (:125). `Gan25` appears three times in the repository (twice here, once in packages/opaque-dpsgd/tests/accounting/test_cross_validation.py:369) and is defined nowhere — no bibliography entry, no arXiv id, no author name. The actual source is Arun Ganesh, "Tighter Privacy Analysis for Truncated Poisson Sampling", arXiv:2508.15089, which appears nowhere in the repository source. The formula itself is faithfully implemented, but the paper's Theorem 3.1 is stated for a RESTRICTED adjacency: "we start with the simplest version of our result, which uses a restricted version of the add-or-remove-1-of-n adjacency ... Our privacy guarantee depends on |D|, so we need to restrict to D,D' pairs of a specific size n." It then warns: "if we are composing M_{B,p,sigma} with other mechanisms, we need to be careful about using this result. Hence, we recommend avoiding the use of this result in these settings." Opaque documents a different convention (docs/user-guide/dp-concepts.md:373 "Opaque uses the **add-or-remove** convention"), states nothing about the n-dependence in docs/reference/accounting.md:238-249, docs/mechanisms/index.md:88 or the factory docstring, and freely composes the truncated process with unrelated mechanisms.
survivors.failure_scenario: A user writes `step = dpsgd_acc.poisson(dpsgd_acc.gaussian(0.8), sample_rate=256/50000, truncated_batch_size=256, dataset_size=50000)` (verbatim the example at docs/reference/accounting.md:250-259) and then composes it with any other release: `acc = Accountant() | step | dpsgd_acc.gaussian(2.0)` runs without warning and reports eps = 1.994 at delta=1e-5 (measured). The published epsilon is only meaningful under add-or-remove-1-of-n with |D| = 50000 treated as public and fixed, and the source explicitly recommends against using the result in exactly this composed setting. A reader who follows the code comment cannot discover this because `[Gan25]` resolves to nothing.

survivors.title: lambda-CGD sensitivity is documented as "Theorem 1, eq 15 of the paper" — Theorem 1's hypotheses do not cover the default normalized mechanism, and eq (15) is a utility metric, not a sensitivity
survivors.claim: The doc says "The sensitivity formula (Theorem 1, eq 15 of the paper) has a closed-form expression in terms of λ, min_sep, and max_participations." In arXiv:2601.22334 (Kalinin, McKenna, Pagh, Lampert, "DP-λCGD"), Theorem 1 is a restatement of Kalinin & Lampert (2024) Theorem 2: "Let C be a lower triangular Toeplitz matrix with decreasing non-negative entries c_0 >= c_1 >= ... >= c_{n-1} >= 0. Then, under b-min-separation, the sensitivity is given by sens_{k,b}(C) = ||sum_{j=0}^{k-1} C[:, jb+1]||_2" — generic, with no closed form in λ. The paper explicitly says of the column-normalized variant (Opaque's DEFAULT, `normalized: bool = True`): "sensitivity Theorem 1 cannot be applied directly. In this work, we generalize the sensitivity theorem specifically for the normalized DP-λCGD in the following theorem. Lemma 8." Eq. (15) is not a sensitivity at all: it is "The squared maximum row l2-norm of the matrix A C_λ^{-1} is ||A C_λ^{-1}||^2_{2→∞} = 1 + (1-λ)^2 (n-1)" — a MaxSE utility quantity inside the proof of Lemma 2. The closed-form λ-CGD sensitivity is eq (14), also inside that proof, and applies to the UNnormalized matrix.
survivors.failure_scenario: A reviewer following the repo's own differential-privacy-review protocol (which requires following the citation to the primary source) opens arXiv:2601.22334, finds Theorem 1 stating a generic min-sep formula for decreasing non-negative Toeplitz matrices, finds eq (15) is a row-norm of the noising matrix, and cannot confirm or refute what `_native().lambda_cgd_normalized_sensitivity_squared(...)` computes. The one sentence that would let them do so — that the default `normalized=True` path is Lemma 8 / eq (12) and `normalized=False` is eq (14) — is absent.

Equation (14), inside the proof of Lemma 2, is the closed-form squared sensitivity of the unnormalized C_lambda, exactly the formula the repo ships; equation (15) is 'The squared maximum row l2-norm of the matrix A C_lambda^{-1} is ||A C_lambda^{-1}||^2_{2->infty} = 1 + (1-lambda)^2 (n-1)', a MaxSE utility quantity. The paper states 'The matrix C_lambda D^{-1} is no longer Toeplitz, and therefore the sensitivity Theorem 1 cannot be applied directly. In this work, we generalize the sensitivity theorem specifically for the normalized DP-lambda-CGD ... Lemma 8 ... (12)'. So docs/mechanisms/dp-ftrl/lambda-cgd.md:70-73 mis-cites on both counts, and the default path is normalized=True (_lambda_cgd.py:171-181 routes to lambda_cgd_normalized_sensitivity_squared). The same mis-citation appears in the Rust header and function docs (matrix_factorization/lambda_cgd.rs:8, :65, :130), where the displayed formula is in fact eq (14); the normalized function there does cite Lemma 8 correctly (:161). Low severity, no epsilon impact - only the pointer a reviewer would follow is wrong. Live gap: citation-repair issue #418 is closed.

survivors.title: BISR implements Lemma 1 with alpha silently pinned to 1 and enforces none of its 0 <= beta < alpha <= 1 hypothesis, while the sibling BSR strategy enforces exactly that hypothesis
survivors.claim: `_bisr_inverse_coefficients_cached` is documented as "BISR inverse square-root coefficients (Lemma 1, arxiv:2505.12128)" and computes `c_k = sum_j r_j * beta^j * r_{k-j}` with the note "For alpha=1". arXiv:2505.12128 Lemma 1 reads "The inverse square root of the matrix A^{-1/2}_{alpha,beta} defined in (4), for 0 <= beta < alpha <= 1, is ... c~_k = sum_{j=0}^{k} r~_j beta^j r~_{k-j} alpha^{k-j}". The code drops the `alpha^{k-j}` factor (valid only at alpha = 1, which it never exposes) and drops the hypothesis: `BisrStrategy.__post_init__` (:163-173) validates only `bandwidth >= 2` and the `inv_coefficients` length, and `beta` is exposed as the unvalidated `momentum` field. `bisr_strategy(bandwidth=4, momentum=1.5)` is accepted. `_bsr.py:72-101` enforces the identical hypothesis for the sibling mechanism with explicit errors, and the Rust `bisr.rs:149-168 validate_common` validates a *different*, Python-unreachable `momentum` argument to `[0, 1)` — the parameter that is checked is the one never passed, and the one that matters is unchecked.
survivors.failure_scenario: `bisr_strategy(bandwidth=4, momentum=1.0)` (a natural carry-over from `band_mf_strategy`, whose `momentum` defaults to 1.0) or `momentum=1.5` is accepted silently. At momentum=1.5, bandwidth=8 the recovered strategy column grows to 2.5e8 over 64 steps instead of decaying, producing a numerically absurd mechanism with no signal to the user. I could NOT turn this into an epsilon error: exhaustive search over all min-sep patterns (n=18, b=3, k=4, beta in {0, 0.9, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0}) shows `bisr_sensitivity_squared` still returns the exact maximum, and the recovered C stays non-negative (so the balls-in-bins Lemma 3.2 hypothesis also survives). The defect is an unenforced documented precondition and an inconsistency with BSR, not a demonstrated privacy break.

survivors.title: from_state_dict(Accountant(budget=...), sd) silently discards the template's budget; budget_exceeded then fails open forever
survivors.claim: The Accountant serializer is registered with `lambda _template, sd: _accountant_from_state_dict(dict(sd))` (line 246) - the template is discarded entirely. `_accountant_state_dict` only writes a `budget` key when `acct._budget is not None` (line 226-227), and `_accountant_from_state_dict` sets `budget = None` unless the saved dict carries one (line 232-234). So `from_state_dict(Accountant(budget=epsilon_budget(...)), saved)` returns an Accountant whose `_budget` is None whenever the checkpoint was written by a run that had no budget (which is every DPTrainer checkpoint - `_dp_trainer.py:1535` constructs `Accountant()` with no budget). `Accountant.budget_exceeded` then hits `if self._budget is None: return False` (line 215-216) and returns False unconditionally, forever. The dispatcher's documented contract ('handlers may ignore it when the dict is self-describing', _dispatch.py:96-107) makes this a silent, by-design drop with no warning and no way for the caller to detect it short of reading `acct._budget` (a private attribute).
survivors.failure_scenario: A two-stage run: stage 1 trains with a fixed `privacy_noise_multiplier` (no budget) and saves `accountant.json`. Stage 2 resumes with an explicit cap - `acct = from_state_dict(Accountant(budget=epsilon_budget(1.0, delta=1e-5)), json.load(f))` - and drives the documented stop loop `for step in ...: acct = acct | step; if acct.budget_exceeded: break`. Reproduced verbatim on the current tree: after 2000 composed Poisson(Gaussian(1.1), q=0.01) steps the restored accountant reports `epsilon_at(1e-5) = 2.1597`, `_budget = None`, `budget_exceeded = False`. The loop never breaks and the run continues past 2.16x its stated epsilon budget with no error, no warning, and no log line. The Accountant class docstring's own resume recipe (lines 73-87) happens to sidestep this by passing `prefix=sft.process` into a fresh `Accountant(budget=budget, ...)`, so the natural one-liner is exactly the unsafe form.
evidence: packages/opaque-accounting/src/opaque/api/accounting/core/_accountant.py:243-247 -> `register_serializer(Accountant, _accountant_state_dict, lambda _template, sd: _accountant_from_state_dict(dict(sd)))` - `_template` is named with a leading underscore and never read.

packages/opaque-accounting/src/opaque/api/accounting/core/_accountant.py:231-235 -> `budget = None; if "budget" in state: budget = budget_from_state_dict(...)` - a checkpoint with no budget key yields budget=None regardless of the template.
packages/opaque-accounting/src/opaque/api/accounting/core/_accountant.py:215-216 -> `if self._budget is None: return False` - the fail-open branch.

packages/opaque-transformers/src/opaque/api/transformers/trainer/_dp_trainer.py:1535 -> `accounting = Accountant()` - DPTrainer never attaches a budget, so every trainer-written accountant.json lacks the key.

Repro (current tree, .venv): `state_dict(a)` -> keys ['process'] only; `b = from_state_dict(Accountant(budget=epsilon_budget(1.0, delta=1e-5)), sd)` -> `b.epsilon_at(1e-5)=2.159739`, `b._budget=None`, `b.budget_exceeded=False`.
survivors.fix_sketch: Have the Accountant from_state_dict handler consult the template: when the saved dict has no `budget` key, keep `template._budget` instead of dropping it. Separately, make `budget_exceeded` distinguish 'no budget configured' from 'budget check unavailable' - e.g. raise (or return None / a tri-state) when the caller asked for a budget that could not be restored, and log at restore time whenever a template budget is being discarded.

survivors.title: Four privacy-relevant kwargs dicts on TrainingArguments accept arbitrary keys silently; the three keys that are read are renames of the underlying public parameter names
survivors.claim: `clipping_kwargs` is read at exactly one site: `ca = a.clipping_kwargs; target_clip_rate = float(ca.get("target_clipping_rate", 0.5)); clip_norm_max = float(ca.get("norm_max", 10.0)); auto_gamma = float(ca.get("gamma", 0.01))`. Every other key is silently discarded. Worse, the two adaptive-clipping keys are *renames* of the public parameters they feed: `target_clipping_rate` -> `adaptive_clipped_grad(target_quantile=...)` and `norm_max` -> `adaptive_clipped_grad(clipping_norm_max=...)`. A user who reads `opaque.dpsgd.adaptive_clipped_grad`'s signature (the documented mechanism API) and writes `clipping_kwargs={"target_quantile": 0.9, "clipping_norm_max": 50.0}` gets a silent no-op. `adaptive_clipped_grad`'s remaining knobs (`learning_rate`, `clipping_norm_min`, `fraction_noise_std`) are unreachable from the trainer at all, and passing them is also silent. The same no-validation pattern applies to `sampling_kwargs` (only `truncated_batch_size`/`max_batch_size`/`total_participations` are ever read), `privacy_noise_mechanism_kwargs` on the gaussian path (filtered to exactly `("bound", "compute_dtype")` at `_dp_trainer.py:1544-1552`), and `noise_calibration_kwargs` (only `min`/`max`/`tolerance`). The same class validates `lr_scheduler_kwargs` strictly - `_scheduler.py:83-91` raises `ValueError` listing the allowed keys - so the inconsistency is internal, not a house style.
survivors.failure_scenario: A user wants adaptive clipping at the 90th percentile with a higher ceiling and configures `TrainingArguments(clipping_mode='adaptive', clipping_kwargs={'target_quantile': 0.9, 'clipping_norm_max': 50.0})`. Construction succeeds with no error and no warning (verified: `a.clipping_kwargs` round-trips the dict untouched). Training runs at `target_quantile=0.5` and `clipping_norm_max=10.0` - a materially different clipping schedule from the one requested, discoverable only by reading the trainer source. Same class of failure for `privacy_noise_mechanism_kwargs={'bounds': (-1.0, 1.0)}` (plural typo of `bound`): accepted, normalized to a list, and dropped by the `_k in ("bound", "compute_dtype")` filter, so an unbounded Gaussian is deployed while the user believes the bounded mechanism is in effect.
evidence: packages/opaque-transformers/src/opaque/api/transformers/trainer/_dp_trainer.py:4145-4148 -> the only three `ca.get(...)` reads; `grep -n 'clipping_kwargs' _dp_trainer.py` returns line 4145 and nothing else.

When `fallback` is supplied - which the trainer's dict form makes mandatory (`clipping_norm` dict 'must include a fallback key', verified by construction) - a misspelled or model-inappropriate substring produces no error, no warning, and no trace in the returned `PerGroup`: the affected parameters just get the fallback bound. survivors.title: compute_loss_func is silently ignored on the default eval path, so eval_loss and best-model selection measure a different objective than training
survivors.claim: `DPTrainer.__init__` stores `compute_loss_func` (line 467) and honours it in `compute_per_example_loss` (line 2320-2322). `prediction_step` reaches that method only when `use_per_example_loss` is true, which requires `"loss" in (self.args.include_for_metrics or [])` (line 2485-2488). `TrainingArguments.include_for_metrics` defaults to an empty list (`_training_arguments.py:364`, `field(default_factory=list)`), so on the default configuration evaluation takes the batched branch and reads the model's own loss directly: `loss = output.get("loss")` (line 2571). No warning is emitted on that branch when `_compute_loss_func` is not None - the only nearby warning (line 2535-2541) fires in the opposite direction. This diverges from `transformers.Trainer`, whose `prediction_step` routes through `compute_loss`, which does apply `compute_loss_func`.
survivors.failure_scenario: A user passes `compute_loss_func=my_weighted_ce` together with `eval_strategy='steps'`, `metric_for_best_model='eval_loss'`, `greater_is_better=False`, `load_best_model_at_end=True` - all fields the class supports. Training minimizes `my_weighted_ce`; the reported `eval_loss` is the HF model's built-in `ForCausalLMLoss`. Checkpoint selection, early-stopping callbacks, and any logged eval curve are therefore driven by an objective the user never asked for, silently. The same branch also skips the `label_smoothing_factor` rebuild that `compute_per_example_loss` applies (line 2299-2340), so `label_smoothing_factor > 0` is likewise absent from the reported eval loss.

packages/opaque-transformers/src/opaque/api/transformers/trainer/_dp_trainer.py:2571 -> batched branch: `loss = output.get("loss")`; `grep -n '_compute_loss_func' _dp_trainer.py` returns only lines 467, 2320, 2322 - it is never consulted on this path.

packages/opaque-transformers/src/opaque/api/transformers/trainer/_dp_trainer.py:2550-2555 -> the comment acknowledges it ('users who want compute_loss_func honoured at eval set include_for_metrics=["loss"]') but the code emits no runtime warning.

survivors.title: set_discretization is a full replace, not a partial update: tuning one knob silently reverts every previously tightened Monte Carlo / grid parameter
survivors.claim: `set_discretization` takes eight parameters, all with library defaults, and assigns `_default_config = DiscretizationConfig(<all eight>)` unconditionally (lines 145-154). It does not read the existing `_default_config`, so any parameter the caller omits is reset to the library default rather than preserved. The docstring calls it 'Set module-level default discretization parameters' and its own worked example - `acc.set_discretization(discretization=1e-3)` (line 132-133) - is exactly the single-knob call shape that silently undoes prior settings. Three of the eight parameters (`discretization`, `mc_resolution`, `mc_failure_probability`) directly move the reported epsilon, and the last two govern the simultaneous confidence band that the b-min-sep and balls-in-bins accountants use - the auto-paired samplers for 5 of the 6 MF mechanisms in `_SAMPLER_BY_MECHANISM`.
survivors.failure_scenario: A team tightens the Monte Carlo band for a DP-FTRL run: `acc.set_discretization(mc_failure_probability=1e-10, mc_resolution=1e-8)`. Later, in the same process (or in a shared setup module), someone coarsens the grid for speed: `acc.set_discretization(discretization=1e-3)`. Reproduced on the current tree: the resulting config is `mc_resolution=1e-05, mc_failure_probability=1e-06` - both silently back at the library defaults, four orders of magnitude looser on the failure probability. Every epsilon computed afterwards is certified at a weaker confidence level than the team configured, with no warning and no diff in any artifact they inspect.
evidence: packages/opaque-accounting/src/opaque/api/accounting/core/discretization.py:145-154 -> `global _default_config; _default_config = DiscretizationConfig(discretization=discretization, ..., mc_failure_probability=mc_failure_probability)` - constructed from the arguments alone, existing state never read.

packages/opaque-accounting/src/opaque/api/accounting/core/discretization.py:132-133 -> docstring example `acc.set_discretization(discretization=1e-3)`, the partial-looking call that triggers the reset.

Repro (current tree): `acc.set_discretization(mc_failure_probability=1e-10, mc_resolution=1e-8)` -> config shows `mc_resolution=1e-08, mc_failure_probability=1e-10`; then `acc.set_discretization(discretization=1e-3)` -> config shows `discretization=0.001, mc_resolution=1e-05, mc_failure_probability=1e-06`.

packages/opaque-accounting/src/opaque/api/accounting/core/discretization.py:36-38 -> `mc_resolution` / `mc_failure_probability` are the Monte Carlo confidence-band parameters; `get_discretization` (keyword-only) is asymmetric with `set_discretization` (positional-or-keyword), reinforcing the impression that the setter is an override rather than a replace.
survivors.fix_sketch: Give every parameter a `None` sentinel and merge onto the current `_default_config` (matching `get_discretization`'s override semantics), or rename to `replace_discretization` / add an explicit `update_discretization`. Making the parameters keyword-only would also match `get_discretization`.

verification.title: Two mechanism pages and the DP-SGD guide instruct accounting the bounded Gaussian with the unbounded accountant; a third page says the accountant does not cover it
verification.reasoning: Every cited line and every measurement reproduces. Docs contradiction is real: gaussian.md:176-177 says 'Treat bound= as experimental: dpsgd_acc.gaussian() does not cover this variant', then gaussian.md:195-198 hands the reader `# Accounting (unchanged from the unbounded mechanism)` with `dpsgd_acc.poisson(dpsgd_acc.gaussian(noise_multiplier), ...)`; dp-sgd.md:95-99 says 'pass bound=... -- same accounting' with no hedge at all; noise.md:177 carries the correct warning while noise.md:146-148 claims 'No probability mass sits at the boundaries'. Implementation checked directly: _gaussian.py:277-285 computes alpha/beta from erf, remaps u into [alpha,beta], inverts, then applies `torch.clamp(sample, min=low, max=high)`. Measured over a 200k-element ClippedPytree(max_norm=1.0) with gaussian_noise(noise_multiplier=1.0, bound=B, key=key(0)): center 0.0/bound 1.0 -> realized sd 0.5409 (reported noise_stddev 1.0); center 5.0/bound 1.0 -> 0.040% of mass exactly at +B, 1060 distinct values, sd 0.2137; center 50.0/bound 1.0 and center 10.0/bound 3.0 -> 100% of mass at the boundary, sd exactly 0.0, one distinct value, i.e. a deterministic zero-noise release at the documented bound=3.0. So noise.md's 'no mass at the boundaries' is false and noise_stddev reports the nominal, not realized, scale. The path is trainer-reachable: _dp_trainer.py:1544-1562 filters privacy_noise_mechanism_kwargs to ('bound','compute_dtype') and functools.partials them into gaussian_noise while the accountant stays the plain Gaussian -- and truncation strictly REDUCES realized noise below what is charged, the unsafe direction. However: issue #344 'Deploy a Gaussian mechanism that matches the accountant' (in the open-issues snapshot; GitHub now shows it closed as not_planned on 2026-08-27) states verbatim that 'The bounded mode ... can collapse outside the interval, and reports a nominal variance that downstream bias correction assumes is realized' while 'accounting prices an unbounded Gaussian', with acceptance criteria 'Extreme centers cannot produce deterministic zero-noise releases' and 'Reported noise metadata matches downstream semantics'. Evidence items (a) and (b) of this finding are that issue restated, so I am marking it tracked under 344 rather than new. The one genuinely untracked slice is the documentation itself -- #344 says nothing about docs -- so gaussian.md:195 and dp-sgd.md:96 will keep instructing an unsound accounting even if #344 stays not_planned; that is a cheap standalone docs fix and should not be lost in the dedup. Severity demoted high -> medium: the mechanism-level privacy defect is #344's, the variant is labelled experimental on two of the four pages, and what remains new here is a documentation contradiction.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A user enables gaussian_noise(..., bound=3.0) -- reachable from DPTrainer via privacy_noise_mechanism_kwargs, which _dp_trainer.py:1544-1562 forwards verbatim -- and calibrates and reports epsilon with `dpsgd_acc.poisson(dpsgd_acc.gaussian(nm), q) * steps`, exactly as gaussian.md:195-198 shows and dp-sgd.md:96 states without qualification. The deployed mechanism is a per-coordinate truncated-and-clamped Gaussian, not the unbounded one the PLD prices, and truncation removes noise rather than adding it: measured at nm=1.0 the realized sd is 0.5409 at bound=1.0 and 0.3400 at bound=3.0/center 5.0, while noise_stddev keeps reporting 1.0 to the optimizer bias correction. When a clipped gradient sum sits well outside the interval -- routine at max_norm=1.0 without normalize_by -- the release collapses to a constant at the boundary (center 10.0, bound 3.0: sd 0.0, one distinct value, 100% of mass at +B), directly contradicting noise.md:146-148's 'No probability mass sits at the boundaries'. Two pages (gaussian.md:176-177, noise.md:177) already warn that dpsgd_acc.gaussian() does not cover this variant, so the docs contradict themselves within the same file.

verification.title: BLT min-sep sensitivity precondition is violated at the DEFAULT momentum=1.0 as soon as an lr_schedule is attached, which the trainer does automatically -- reported sensitivity 1.45-1.54x too small at min_sep=1
verification.reasoning: The numerical claim reproduces exactly. I re-derived the true sensitivity by exhaustive enumeration of every min-sep-respecting participation set against the lower-triangular Toeplitz C built from _blt_toeplitz_coefs: at max_buffers=10, momentum=1.0, n=20, min_sep=1 -- no schedule 4.47214 vs 4.47214 (1.0000); linear_schedule coefficient min -0.160402, reported 1.86202 vs true 2.69864 (1.4493); cosine_schedule coefficient min -0.183244, reported 1.75101 vs true 2.69688 (1.5402). At min_sep=2 ratios collapse to 1.0001, at min_sep=3 to 1.0000. So the Theorem 2 precondition (arXiv:2405.13763; non-negative non-increasing Toeplitz coefficients) is violated at the default momentum once a schedule is attached, and _blt.py:185-192 evaluates it with skip_checks=True. But this is the same defect, same call site, and same fix as OPEN issue #595, whose acceptance criterion is configuration-agnostic and resolves this case too; #595 already records a larger 2.03x under-report, so this is not a materially worse instance. I also refuted the reachability half of the headline: the trainer does inject lr_schedule for mf_blt (_dpftrl.py:87,113-118), but mf_blt's only allowed sampler is balls_in_bins (_ALLOWED_SAMPLERS), and BallsInBins uses min_sep=num_bins (_balls_in_bins.py:98) and for BltStrategy routes through toeplitz_gram_matrix/bnb_mc_pld without ever calling strategy.sensitivity(). b_min_sep only accepts BandMfStrategy and poisson rejects BLT outright, so the affected path is reachable only through a bare mf_gaussian(nm, blt_strategy(lr_schedule=...), n_steps=N, min_sep=1, max_participations>1) call in the functional API -- narrower than 'the trainer does this automatically'.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: A functional-API user builds blt_strategy(max_buffers=10, momentum=1.0, lr_schedule=linear_schedule(...)) -- momentum=1.0 is the default -- and accounts it with dpftrl_acc.mf_gaussian(nm, strategy, n_steps=20, min_sep=1). The optimized Toeplitz coefficients go negative (min -0.1604 linear, -0.1832 cosine) and non-monotone, so minsep_sensitivity_squared, called with skip_checks=True at _blt.py:185-192, is evaluated outside the hypothesis of Theorem 2 of arXiv:2405.13763 and stops being an upper bound: reported S = 1.86202 vs exhaustively-verified true S = 2.69864 (1.449x; cosine 1.75101 vs 2.69688, 1.540x). Since MfGaussian.pld sets effective_nm = nm / S, epsilon is under-reported. The gap vanishes at min_sep >= 2 (1.0001) and 3 (1.0000), and the HF trainer path is not affected at all: mf_blt is pinned to balls_in_bins, which uses min_sep = num_bins and, for BLT, reaches the PLD through toeplitz_gram_matrix/bnb_mc_pld without calling strategy.sensitivity(). Same defect and same fix as open issue #595, at a lower ratio than the 2.03x already recorded there.

trackedDupes.title: mu-GDP one-run audit substitutes v_k = 0.5 for every rank past 2000 and calls it "conservative" — it is the anti-conservative direction under Xiang et al. Theorem 3, inflating the audited mu lower bound
trackedDupes.claim: `_p_value` computes exact `v_k` for only `r_prime = min(r, _MAX_EXACT_RANKS)` ranks and sets `n_trunc = r - r_prime` ranks to `v_k = 0.5`, annotated `# truncated ranks use v_k = 0.5 (conservative)` (:38, :333). The bound is cited as "Xiang et al. 2025, Theorem 3" (:377) with `v_k` from "Eq. 12" (:342). arXiv:2509.08704 Theorem 3 states `Pr[event_u] <= Pr[sum_{k=n-r+1}^{n} V_k <= u]` with `V_k ~ Bernoulli(v_k)` and `v_k` given by its Eq. (25) (which `_compute_v_k` reproduces correctly). Because `sigmoid(-|L|) <= 0.5` always, `v_k <= 0.5`, so 0.5 is an UPPER bound on each true `v_k`; `Pr[sum V_k <= u]` is monotonically DECREASING in the `v_k`, so the substitution makes the computed p-value SMALLER than the true bound — it is no longer an upper bound on `Pr[event_u]` and is not a valid p-value. `_mu_at` returns `mu_lo`, the largest mu at which the p-value stays below `significance` (the largest rejected mu), so an under-stated p-value rejects too much and reports an inflated mu-hat. The comment at :37-39 ("Truncated low-confidence ranks use v_k = 0.5 (conservative). ... covers the top 20 % for n = 10K, which dominates the Chernoff sum") is wrong on both counts: the substitution is anti-conservative, and the truncated block dominates the sum (measured 3000.0 vs 193.3 at n=20000, r=8000, mu=1).
trackedDupes.failure_scenario: `_best_r_u` always returns `r = m = n_in + n_out` (_estimate.py:147, 152, 161), so any audit with more than 2000 canaries truncates. Measured at significance 0.05: with m = r = 3000 canaries and u = 900 errors, the shipped code reports mu-hat = 1.0563 while the same search with exact `v_k` gives 0.9313. With r = 4000, u = 1100, n = 20000 the gap is 1.0688 vs 0.4875 — a 2.2x inflation of the audited mu. At the p-value level, n=20000, r=8000, mu=1.0, u=1396: exact p-value 0.0909 (would NOT reject at 0.05) vs truncated 0.0 (rejects). Because docs/user-guide/auditing.md:5-6 tells users "If the audited epsilon exceeds the theoretical epsilon, there is likely a bug in the implementation", the consequence is a false privacy-violation alarm on a correct implementation; in the strong-attack regime the same defect makes the p-value stay below significance for every finite mu and `_mu_at` raises RuntimeError instead (:80-89).

Delta-window commit 611faf51 ("fix(auditing): cap mu-GDP _mu_at search to stop infinite hang", #299) touched exactly this code, added a `Raises: RuntimeError ... which truncated ranks (v_k = 0.5) can cause` docstring, and left the wrong-direction bound and the "(conservative)" comment in place

verification.title: mu-GDP one-run audit substitutes v_k = 0.5 for every rank past 2000 and calls it "conservative" - it is the anti-conservative direction under Xiang et al. Theorem 3
verification.reasoning: Reproduced exactly. _gdp.py:329-334 caps exact ranks at _MAX_EXACT_RANKS=2000 and passes n_trunc = r - r' ranks to _chernoff_lower_tail as Bernoulli(0.5); _compute_v_k:368 clips v_k into [0, 0.5], so 0.5 is an upper bound on every true v_k, and Pr[sum V_k <= u] is decreasing in the v_k - the substitution therefore makes the computed p-value smaller than the Theorem-3 bound it must over-estimate, so it is not a valid p-value. Measured with the shipped functions (n=20000, r=8000, mu=1.0, u=1396): truncated p-value 0.0 vs exact 0.0909 - rejects where the valid bound does not. The comment's rationale is measurably false too: exact top-2000 sum of v_k = 193.34, substituted block = 3000.0, true sum over all 8000 ranks = 1470.4, so the truncated block dominates rather than the kept one. End to end, _best_r_u always returns r = m (_estimate.py:147-161), so any audit with more than 2000 canaries truncates; replaying _mu_at with and without the cap at significance 0.05 gives m=r=3000, u=900 -> 1.0538 shipped vs 0.9277 exact, and n=20000, r=4000, u=1100 -> 1.0689 vs 0.4919. Severity dropped from high to medium: the only direction of the error is an inflated audited mu-hat / epsilon lower bound - the audit over-states leakage (false alarm on a correct implementation, or the RuntimeError path at :80-89) and can never hide a real privacy loss. Duplicate of open #376 'Calibrate one-run auditing under the null', whose body names 'truncated-rank bounds are not calibrated for large audits' and whose acceptance criteria include 'Large-m truncation is exercised and conservative relative to a higher exact-rank limit'.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: Any one-run audit with more than 2000 canaries (r = m always) prices the remaining r-2000 ranks at v_k = 0.5, an upper bound on each true v_k, which pushes the Chernoff p-value below the Theorem-3 bound it must upper-bound. verification.title: Trainer accountant.json save crashes with RecursionError for composition spines deeper than ~1000
verification.reasoning: The cited line is guarded and the reporter's repro omitted the guard. _dp_trainer.py:4994-4995 reads `with path.open("w") as f, _deep_json_recursion():` / `json.dump(opaque_state_dict(accountant), f)` - the json.dump is inside a context manager, not bare. _deep_json_recursion is defined at _dp_trainer.py:334-358: it raises sys.setrecursionlimit to 30_000 for the duration and restores the previous value in a finally block, with a docstring documenting exactly this failure mode ('stdlib json's C encoder/scanner still recurse once per nesting level and hit the default limit near ~1000') and explaining why 30k rather than higher. The load path is guarded identically at _dp_trainer.py:5183. git log -L334,336 shows the guard landed in 6a3ccb64, 'fix(accounting): serialize, load, compare, and repr deep compositions iteratively (#544)', an ancestor of 4b13d82 and untouched by HEAD commit 50402c8c (which only adds audit scratch files). I verified sufficiency at the claimed depth: a 3000-level nested dict raises RecursionError at the default limit and both serializes and round-trips cleanly (90000 bytes, json.loads OK) at limit 30000. Closed #334 therefore did land a working fix at the exact line cited; the reporter reproduced RecursionError by calling json.dumps outside the trainer's context manager, which no production path does.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: No failure. The trainer's accountant.json save at _dp_trainer.py:4995 runs inside `_deep_json_recursion()` (defined at :334), which temporarily raises the recursion limit to 30_000 and restores it on exit; the checkpoint load path at :5183 does the same. I confirmed a 3000-level nested wire dict fails json.dumps at the default limit of 1000 and succeeds (dump and load) at 30_000, so heterogeneous spines up to roughly 25k steps checkpoint normally. The reported RecursionError occurs only when json.dumps is called directly on the state dict without the trainer's guard.

A user who sets DiscretizationConfig.tail_mass_truncation coarse (e.g. 1e-3, a public field) widens the inconsistency proportionally in the trade-off curve while delta_at stays consistent.

metrics.rs:297: '// No negative_infinity_mass: it's absorbed by the renormalization to' and :306 '// from cleaned probabilities. No negative_infinity_mass added.' (asymmetric path, unchanged)
git diff 79c916e3..4b13d82 -- packages/opaque-accounting/src/pld/metrics.rs shows only the new infinity_mass() helper and Pmf constructor-signature churn in tests

verification.title: Closed #338 (OPQ-181) not fixed: asymmetric beta still drops negative_infinity_mass
verification.reasoning: The code observation is accurate but the finding does not hold as a defect. (a) Record: issue #338 was closed with state_reason=not_planned and an explicit withdrawal comment - 'The apparent symmetric/asymmetric handling difference is not, by itself, evidence of a metric bug; the proposed regression used uncoupled synthetic PMFs and could not establish the required PLD correspondence. Any future work should start from a valid mechanism-generated asymmetric PLD and an independent derivation or reference result.' So 'closed but not fixed' mischaracterizes the record: it was deliberately declined, never claimed fixed. Re-filing it without the evidence the maintainer asked for is exactly the wasted engineer-day this pass exists to prevent. (b) The finding supplies no mechanism-generated asymmetric PLD on which beta_at and delta_at actually disagree - the same gap that got #338 withdrawn. (c) Direction: I checked the arithmetic. Symmetric (metrics.rs:216) sets cdf_y[0] = neginf + p0; asymmetric (metrics.rs:293-306) uses clean_probs (metrics.rs:126-137), which renormalizes to 1 - infinity_mass, giving cdf_y[0] = p0*(1-inf)/(1-inf-neginf) ~= p0 + p0*neginf <= neginf + p0 since p0 <= 1. The asymmetric path therefore yields a SMALLER beta - it claims less privacy, i.e. errs in the CONSERVATIVE direction, which is never critical. (d) Magnitude: I confirmed the reporter's own bound - MC PLDs fail closed in beta_at (pld/mod.rs:355-357, `if self.estimation_failure_probability > 0.0 { return 0.0 }`), and for analytic asymmetric PLDs negative_infinity_mass is capped by left_tail_budget (pld/pmf/dense.rs:312), i.e. tail_mass_truncation/2 = 5e-16 by default. The discrepancy is at floating-point noise level, and only a deliberately coarse tail_mass_truncation widens it - still conservatively.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: No demonstrated failure. pmf_beta and pmf_beta_asymmetric do treat negative_infinity_mass differently (added at cdf_y[0] vs renormalized away by clean_probs), and no beta_at/delta_at correspondence test exists. But the asymmetric treatment is the conservative one (it lowers beta), delta_at/epsilon_at are untouched, MC PLDs already fail closed in beta_at, and the reachable negative-infinity mass on analytic asymmetric PLDs is bounded by the default left tail budget of 5e-16 - so no user-visible trade-off-curve error was produced or is producible at defaults. Issue #338 was withdrawn as not-a-bug on exactly this evidence gap.

refuted.title: Coin flips are positional and invariant to the canary pool, enabling silent audit invalidation under key reuse
refuted.claim: The in/out coin mask is a pure function of (key, num_canaries) — `coin_rng = np.random.default_rng(fold_in(key, _COIN_FLIP_DOMAIN).seed); in_mask = coin_rng.random(num_canaries) < 0.5` — so it is byte-identical across every candidate_indices value (pinned as intended behavior by tests/auditing/test_audit.py:467 `np.testing.assert_array_equal(pooled._in_mask, expected_mask)`), prefix-stable across num_canaries, and fully caller-computable before the pool is committed. Coins are then assigned to records positionally through the selection permutation of np.unique(pool). This makes the one-run fair-coin independence assumption unverifiable and easy to violate silently whenever a key is reused across pool iterations, which the docs themselves encourage (every snippet uses key(42)).
refuted.failure_scenario: (a) Inflation/false alarm: a caller (or an automated canary-crafting loop) that computes the deterministic record→coin map before training — reproduced in 6 lines from public API — and correlates canary content with the precomputed coin (e.g. places duplicates of always-in rows at coin=in indices and OOD garbage at coin=out indices) gets honest loss_scores that separate perfectly regardless of DP noise. Demonstrated end-to-end: for a mechanism with ZERO leakage (scores set equal to the precomputed coins via public canary_scores), one_run reports eps_delta().epsilon_at(delta=0) = 5.81 and gdp epsilon_at(delta=1e-5) = 38.2 at m=1000 — the audit 'lower bound' exceeds any real guarantee. (b) Silent corruption on drift: editing the pool by ONE element under the same key reassigns in/out for ~half the shared records (measured 45/100 flipped between candidate_indices=range(1000,1100) and range(1000,1101)). A workflow that recreates the partition in a separate eval script (natural, since coin_flip is documented as 'reproducible' from the key) with a pool that drifted by one record silently splits honest scores against membership labels that are ~uncorrelated with the ones used in training — one_run raises nothing and reports a meaningless epsilon in either direction.
evidence: packages/opaque-auditing/src/opaque/api/auditing/_coin_flip.py:353-358: `rng = np.random.default_rng(fold_in(key, _CANARY_SELECTION_DOMAIN).seed); canary_indices = rng.choice(population, size=num_canaries, replace=False); coin_rng = np.random.default_rng(fold_in(key, _COIN_FLIP_DOMAIN).seed); in_mask = np.asarray(coin_rng.random(num_canaries) < _INCLUSION_PROBABILITY, dtype=bool)` — coin stream never sees the pool or the selected identities.

packages/opaque-auditing/tests/auditing/test_audit.py:440-467: test_coin_flip_uses_reproducible_domain_separated_keys asserts `pooled._in_mask == expected_mask` where pooled uses candidate_indices=range(50,100) and expected_mask comes from the un-pooled call — the invariance is test-pinned.

Empirical (run in this session, commit 4b13d82): mask full==poolA True; mask full==poolB True (pool sizes 100 and 101); records whose in/out flipped after adding one pool element: 45 of 100; caller-side coin prediction from fold_in(key,'opaque.auditing.canary_selection')/'opaque.auditing.coin_flip' matches cf.in_indices exactly; coin stream prefix-stable across num_canaries (mask[:100] of m=200 equals mask of m=100).

Empirical inflation demo: cf2 = coin_flip(ds, num_canaries=1000, key=key(42), candidate_indices=range(1000)); scores = 1.0 where index in cf2.in_indices else 0.0; one_run(canary_scores(...), coin_flip=cf2) → eps_delta epsilon_at(delta=0) = 5.809, gdp epsilon_at(delta=1e-5) = 38.25 — with scores that contain no information about any training run.

docs/user-guide/auditing.md (Stronger canaries): 'Fix the pool before target training, independently of that run's membership coins' — an obligation the API makes uncheckable (the coins are a deterministic public function of key and num_canaries, computable before the pool is fixed) and does not detect violations of.

One-run validity requires the membership coins to be uniform and independent of the guessing strategy/canary choice: Steinke, Nasr, Jagielski (2023), arXiv:2305.08846, Theorem 5.2 (coins S_i i.i.d. and independent of everything the adversary controls); the same assumption carries into Xiang et al. (2025), arXiv:2509.08704.
refuted.fix_sketch: Fold the canonicalized selected canary identities (or a hash of the validated pool) into the coin-flip domain — e.g. fold_in(key, _COIN_FLIP_DOMAIN, blake2-of-sorted-pool) — so any pool or num_canaries change rerandomizes all coins, invalidating precomputed coin knowledge across pool iterations; additionally record a fingerprint (dataset_size, pool hash) on CoinFlip and provide serialization so eval scripts reload the training-time partition instead of recreating it; document that the audit key must be drawn fresh after the pool is committed and never reused across pool designs.

verification.title: Coin flips are positional and invariant to the canary pool, enabling silent audit invalidation under key reuse
verification.reasoning: Every mechanical fact reproduces (I ran it): _coin_flip.py:353-358 derives the positional mask from fold_in(key, 'opaque.auditing.coin_flip') only, so mask(full)==mask(poolA)==mask(poolB) is True, the mask is prefix-stable across num_canaries (mask[:100] of m=200 == mask of m=100), and adding one pool element flipped 45 of the 99 shared records' in/out labels. But none of that establishes a library defect. (a) The inflation demo is self-cheating: the record->coin map is NOT pool-invariant - coins bind to records only through rng.choice over the pool, so the map is computable only AFTER the pool is fixed, and the demo's 'zero-leakage mechanism' is scores set equal to the coins. An auditor who deliberately correlates canary content with coins they hold the key for breaks one-run validity in every implementation including the reference one; Steinke et al. Thm 5.2 assumes the coins are drawn independently of the canaries, and the library supports exactly that ordering (coin_flip is called on a dataset that already exists). docs/user-guide/auditing.md:273-277 states the obligation explicitly ('Fix the pool before target training, independently of that run's membership coins and outputs; do not construct CoinFlip directly to choose a favourable in/out mask'). (b) The drift scenario is ordinary seeded-reproducibility semantics under a user error the same paragraph forbids ('Use the same audited dataset for coin_flip, subset construction, and scoring'): changing candidate_indices changes both the selection and the labels, as any seeded partition does. The coin stream is correctly domain-separated from mechanism keys (test_audit.py:440-467 asserts three distinct roots; test_stream_root_namespacing.py enumerates both auditing tags). A legitimate hardening exists - deriving each coin as fold_in(coin_root, record_index) so pool drift perturbs only the added/removed records - but that is an improvement, not a defect, and no honest documented usage produces a wrong epsilon.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: No honest-usage failure established. Reproduced facts: the positional in/out mask is a pure function of (key, num_canaries), byte-identical across candidate_indices values and prefix-stable across num_canaries; because coins attach to records positionally through the pool-dependent selection permutation, editing the pool by one element reassigns in/out for ~half the shared records (45/99 measured). Both claimed consequences require the caller to violate an explicitly documented obligation - correlating canary content with coins they hold the key for, or recreating the partition against a drifted pool - and neither is reachable from the documented workflow. Available hardening: identity-bound coin derivation (fold_in(coin_root, record_index)) to localize drift; the current design is not itself incorrect.

refuted.title: The K-prefix invariant sweep was thinned to 4 sampled steps, dropping K=n-1 and every atomic-unit boundary, in the exact area covered by 8 open prefix-accounting issues

For a typical pair (n=80, M=8) that is 10 monotonicity points down to 3. K=n-1 - the tightest prefix and the one an off-by-one between prefix and horizon would break first - is no longer checked at all. `test_prefix_invariants` carries `@pytest.mark.slow` (line 449), so it is deselected from every PR lane and only runs on main - the thinning removes points from the one gate that does run it.

refuted.title: docs/limitations.md, the page the user guide links as the safety page, contains no privacy-correctness limitation at all while high-severity ones are tracked open and other pages assert the opposite
refuted.claim: Every one of limitations.md's nine sections is a functional/compatibility limitation (MF workload-utility, PRNG threat model, telemetry, gradient checkpointing, Flash Attention 2, DDP-only, kernel patching, vmap in-place, vmap control flow). Not one tracked privacy-correctness limitation appears: BandMF sensitivity being participation-blind (#359), the BLT min-sep precondition not being enforced (#595), nothing binding the runtime sampler to the amplifier (#320/#356), and the bounded-Gaussian sampler not matching any accountant (#344). refuted.title: with_restarts reuses the name transition_steps for the total span across all cycles, silently double-specifying the length against the base schedule it wraps
refuted.claim: In every base factory in `opaque.scheduling` (`linear_schedule`, `cosine_schedule`, `polynomial_schedule`, ...) `transition_steps` is the length of one decay. In `with_warmup` it is the warmup length. In `with_restarts` it is the *total* span of all cycles, and the per-cycle length is the derived `transition_steps / num_cycles` (line 39). The wrapper never compares that derived cycle length to the inner schedule's own `transition_steps`, so a mismatch is silent: the inner schedule is simply evaluated over a truncated (or over-extended) domain, and past the total span `WithRestarts` returns the constant `self.schedule(cycle_length)` (line 43-44). The trainer builds the pair correctly (`_scheduler.py:200-215` constructs a `CosineSchedule` with `transition_steps = decay_steps / cycles` before wrapping), which is exactly the coupling a direct caller has to rediscover.
refuted.failure_scenario: A user writes the natural composition `with_restarts(cosine_schedule(1.0, 0.0, transition_steps=1000), transition_steps=1000, num_cycles=4)` expecting four 1000-step cosine cycles. verification.title: with_restarts reuses the name transition_steps for the total span across all cycles, silently double-specifying the length against the base schedule it wraps
verification.reasoning: The arithmetic reproduces exactly (`with_restarts(linear_schedule(1.0,0.0,10), 5, 3)` -> [1.0, 0.9, 0.967, 0.867, 0.933, 0.833, 0.833, ...]), but the behavior is the documented contract, not a defect. (1) `WithRestarts.__doc__` (_with_restarts.py:16-31) states 'Each cycle has (real-valued) length transition_steps / num_cycles; within a cycle, schedule is evaluated at the cycle-local position' and 'after the final cycle, returns schedule(cycle_length)'. (2) docs/reference/schedules.md:316-343 repeats this and adds the explicit instruction 'Configure `schedule` to produce its full curve over a single cycle of that length', followed by a worked SGDR example that sets `inner = cosine_schedule(1e-3, 0.0, transition_steps=1000)` with `with_restarts(inner, transition_steps=4000, num_cycles=4)`. (3) docs/user-guide/lr-scheduling.md:139-158 shows the same pairing and even names the intermediate `cycle_length = N / k`. So the coupling is not something 'a direct caller has to rediscover' from the trainer source - it is stated in the reference page, the user guide, and the class docstring, each with the correct composition spelled out. (4) The proposed validation is not implementable in general: `Schedule` is a bare `Callable[[int], float]` type alias (_schedule.py:16), not a protocol with a length attribute; several supported inners (constant_schedule, exponential/inverse_sqrt where `transition_steps` means a timescale or decay period, or any user lambda) have no 'full curve length' to compare against, so a duck-typed check would fire spuriously or not at all. (5) The 'overloaded name' premise is also weak: in `with_warmup` and in every recipe, `transition_steps` is the length of the interval that object governs; for `with_restarts` the governed interval is the whole restart window, which is consistent rather than a redefinition. (6) Behavior is pinned by tests (packages/opaque-engine/tests/scheduling/test_scheduling.py:369-411 including `test_after_window_returns_cycle_end`) and by HF-parity tests at :480-510; the only in-repo consumer (_scheduler.py:203-221) composes correctly and deliberately preserves a fractional inner span for HF parity. No privacy surface: schedules only scale the learning rate, never sensitivity, noise, or accounting inputs, so affects_epsilon=false is correct. Nothing in issues-open.tsv covers LR scheduling. Net: a documented-usage ergonomics preference (add an optional cycle-length assertion), not a defect an engineer should be dispatched to fix.
verification.corrected_failure_scenario: No defect established. A caller who passes an inner schedule whose own span differs from `transition_steps / num_cycles` gets a truncated or over-extended curve per cycle, e.g. `with_restarts(cosine_schedule(1.0,0.0,1000), transition_steps=1000, num_cycles=4)` yields four windows traversing only the first quarter of the cosine (values 1.0 -> 0.855 across each 250-step window) and a flat 0.8536 tail from step 1000. But this is the behavior the class docstring, docs/reference/schedules.md:316-343 and docs/user-guide/lr-scheduling.md:139-158 all document, each showing the correct pairing (`inner` built with `transition_steps = total / num_cycles`); the correctly composed form was verified to give the intended SGDR shape (1.0, 0.5, 0.0 per 250-step cycle). No generic guard is possible because `Schedule` is a plain `Callable[[int], float]` with no length attribute, and several supported inner recipes have no comparable span. Utility-only in any case; no effect on sensitivity, noise, or accounting.
